modules.title: Understand Your Productivity Patterns
modules.summary: Before you build anything, you look honestly at where your current way of working breaks down. This module turns vague frustration into a clear picture you can design around.

lessons.title: Why Productivity Systems Fail
lessons.summary: Why most systems collapse, and the five questions a system you can actually return to must answer.

sections.what: A look at the real reasons productivity systems stop working, and the five questions any useful system has to answer.
sections.why: If you know why past systems failed, you can stop blaming yourself and start removing the friction instead.
sections.do: List three parts of your current system that create friction.
sections.output: A short list of three friction points in your current system

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Most productivity systems do not fail because the person using them is lazy or broken. They fail because the system asks for too much. Usually it is one of four things:

- **Too many decisions.** Every time you open the system, you have to decide where things go, what colour to use, which list is which.
- **Too many steps.** Writing down one task takes five clicks or three notebooks.
- **Too much maintenance.** The system only works if you update it daily, and the first missed day leaves it out of date.
- **Too much consistency.** It assumes every day looks the same. Real life does not.

When a system needs perfect behaviour, any normal messy week breaks it. Then it feels easier to abandon it and start a new one.

The goal of this course is different. You are not building the most impressive system. You are building one you can **return to** when life gets messy, even after a week away.

A useful system answers five questions quickly:

1. What do I need to remember?
2. What matters now?
3. What is the next action?
4. When will I work on it?
5. What needs reviewing?

If your current setup cannot answer one of these in under a minute, that is a gap, not a personal failing. Each module in this course fills one of these gaps with the lowest-friction tool that does the job.

> Make the next action obvious. Everything else is optional.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Thandi uses a beautiful planner with colour-coded tabs, a habit tracker and a separate app for work tasks. It worked for two weeks. Then she had a busy weekend, skipped three days, and the planner felt like a record of failure. She went back to keeping things in her head.

When she listed the friction, it was clear:

1. Two places to check (planner and app), so she never knew which was current.
2. The habit tracker needed daily ticking, so one gap made it feel useless.
3. Colour-coding meant stopping to find the right pen before writing anything.

None of these were about willpower. They were design problems.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Take five minutes. Think about the way you currently keep track of tasks, even if that is "in my head" or "sticky notes everywhere".

1. Open your Personal Productivity Profile.
2. In the first field, list **three parts of your current system that create friction**. Be specific: "I have to search three apps" is more useful than "I'm disorganised".
3. For each one, ask: is this too many decisions, too many steps, too much maintenance, or too much consistency?

You will fill in the rest of the profile in the next two lessons.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, notice one moment when you avoid your system. Maybe you skip writing something down, or you avoid opening a list. When it happens, ask "What made that annoying?" and add the answer to your friction list.

You are collecting evidence, not judging yourself. The more specific the friction, the easier it is to design it out in later modules.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a productivity system?
options: To make important actions easier to identify and execute
questions.explain: A system exists to make the important next action easy to see and easy to do. Scheduling every minute or maximising hours adds pressure without adding clarity.

questions.q: A system works well for two weeks and is abandoned after one busy weekend. What is the most likely cause?
options: The system needed too much maintenance or consistency
questions.explain: Systems that only work with daily upkeep break the first time life gets messy. That is a design problem you can fix.

sections.markdown:
- You know the four common reasons productivity systems fail.
- You know the five questions a useful system must answer.
- You have listed three specific friction points in your current system.

lessons.title: Your Productivity Friction Audit
lessons.summary: Rate ten areas of your work to find exactly where things break down.

sections.what: A quick audit that rates ten areas where work tends to break down, from capturing tasks to your physical environment.
sections.why: Most people try to fix everything at once. Finding your top three friction areas tells you where small changes will help most.
sections.do: Rate each of the ten areas from 1 to 5 and pick your three highest-friction areas.
sections.output: Ten friction ratings and your top three problem areas

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Work does not break down in one big way. It breaks at specific points. The audit looks at ten of them:

- **Capture**: getting tasks and ideas out of your head and somewhere safe.
- **Organization**: knowing where things live and finding them again.
- **Prioritization**: deciding what matters most right now.
- **Starting**: crossing the gap between "I should" and actually beginning.
- **Focus**: staying with one thing long enough to make progress.
- **Time estimation**: knowing roughly how long things take.
- **Scheduling**: giving important work a real place in your day.
- **Completion**: finishing the last 10% and closing things off.
- **Reviewing**: checking back so nothing quietly slips.
- **Environment**: your desk, phone, tabs and noise.

Rate each area from 1 to 5, where **1 means it rarely causes problems** and **5 means it causes problems often**. Go with your first honest answer. You are describing a typical week, not your best or worst one.

Then pick the **three highest-friction areas**. If several share a score, choose the ones that cost you the most: missed deadlines, stress, or lost time.

Your top three become your focus for this course. You will still work through every module, but you will know which tools deserve extra attention, and which modules to revisit first when things slip.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sipho's ratings looked like this: Capture 4, Organization 3, Prioritization 2, Starting 5, Focus 4, Time estimation 5, Scheduling 3, Completion 2, Reviewing 4, Environment 3.

His top three: **Starting, Time estimation, Focus.**

That told him something useful. He was not bad at knowing what mattered (prioritization scored 2). His problem was getting going and underestimating how long things took. So Modules 5 and 6 became his priority, and he planned to pay extra attention to buffers when scheduling.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Personal Productivity Profile and complete the friction audit section.

1. Rate each of the ten areas from 1 to 5. Take no more than 20 seconds per area.
2. Look at your highest scores.
3. Write your **three highest-friction areas** in the "Top three" field, most costly first.

If you are stuck between two scores, pick the higher one. Underrating friction is more common than overrating it.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the next few days, keep your top three in mind. When something goes wrong, check whether it falls into one of them. If a different area keeps showing up, update your ratings. The audit is a living document, not a test score.

Write your top three somewhere you will see them, such as the first page of your notebook or a note on your phone's home screen.

questions.q: In the friction audit, what does a rating of 5 mean?
options: This area does not apply to me
This area is a medium concern
questions.explain: The scale runs from 1 (rarely a problem) to 5 (often a problem), so high scores point to where help is most needed.

questions.q: Why pick only three highest-friction areas?
options: So you can focus effort where small changes help most
Because the course only covers three areas
questions.explain: Trying to fix everything at once adds friction. Three clear priorities show you where to put attention first.

sections.markdown:
- You have rated all ten friction areas.
- You have named your top three friction areas.
- You know which modules to lean on most.

lessons.title: Build Your Personal Productivity Profile
lessons.summary: Record your distractions, energy patterns and what has and hasn't worked for you before.

sections.what: A one-page profile of how you actually work: your distractions, energy, avoided tasks and past planning methods.
sections.why: The rest of the course asks you to make choices. Your profile makes those choices fit you, not an imaginary perfect person.
sections.do: Fill in each section of your Personal Productivity Profile using real examples from the last few weeks.
sections.output: Your completed Personal Productivity Profile

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Generic advice assumes everyone works the same way. You don't. Your profile captures the patterns that matter when designing your system. It covers seven things:

- **Common distractions.** What pulls you away? Phone, messages, news, noise, other people, your own thoughts?
- **Typical energy patterns.** When do you usually feel sharp, flat or restless? Morning, after lunch, late at night?
- **Tasks you avoid.** Which kinds of tasks sit on your list for weeks? Phone calls, admin, writing, money tasks?
- **Situations where you focus well.** Where and when has focus come more easily? A café, a deadline, someone else in the room, music?
- **Things you frequently forget.** Bills, replies, appointments, items to buy, where you put things?
- **Planning methods that have failed.** Which apps, planners or routines did you drop, and why?
- **Planning methods that have helped.** Even partly. A whiteboard, a friend checking in, alarms, a single paper list?

Be specific and be kind. This is not a list of flaws. It is data. "I avoid phone calls because I don't know what to say" is far more useful than "I procrastinate".

Pay special attention to what **has helped**, even a little. Those are clues. A method that worked for a week is not a failure; it tells you something about what suits you. Later modules will build on those clues.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Part of Lerato's profile:

- **Distractions:** WhatsApp groups, checking email "just quickly", tidying when a task feels hard.
- **Energy:** Sharpest from 9 to 11am. Flat after lunch. A second wind around 7pm.
- **Avoided tasks:** Calling the bank, filling in forms, starting reports.
- **Focus well when:** Working at the library, with a clear deadline, or on a video call with a friend who is also working.
- **Forgets:** Replying to messages, renewing things, where she saved files.
- **Failed:** A complex app with tags and projects.
- **Helped:** One sticky note with three tasks on her laptop.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Personal Productivity Profile and complete the profile fields.

1. For each section, add at least two items.
2. Use real examples from the last two to three weeks.
3. In "Planning methods that have helped", include anything that worked even for a few days.
4. Write one sentence summary: "I work best when..."

Ten to fifteen minutes is enough. You can add to it later.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep your profile open this week. When you notice a new distraction, an energy dip or something you forgot, add it. By the end of the week your profile will be more accurate than any personality test.

You will use it directly in later modules: your distractions in Module 6, your avoided tasks in Module 5, and your helpful methods throughout.

questions.q: Which entry is most useful in a Productivity Profile?
options: I avoid phone calls because I don't know what to say first
questions.explain: Specific entries point to a solution. Knowing the call feels hard because the opening is unclear suggests writing the first sentence in advance.

questions.q: Why record planning methods that helped only for a short time?
options: They show what suits you and can be rebuilt with less friction
So you never use them again
questions.explain: A method that worked briefly contains a clue about what helps you. The aim is to keep the useful part and remove what made it hard to keep up.

sections.markdown:
- You have recorded your distractions, energy patterns and avoided tasks.
- You have noted where you focus well and what you often forget.
- You have listed what has failed and what has helped.
- Your Personal Productivity Profile is complete.

modules.title: Capture Everything
modules.summary: You get everything that is taking up mental space out of your head and into one trusted place. This frees attention for actually doing things.
modules.outcome: One trusted capture system: your Master Capture List

lessons.title: The Open-Loop Problem
lessons.summary: Why unfinished tasks keep pulling at your attention, and how capture releases them.

sections.what: An explanation of open loops: unfinished things your mind keeps trying to hold on to.
sections.why: Every open loop you carry in your head competes for attention. Capturing it means you can stop rehearsing it.
sections.do: Do a full 10-minute brain dump of everything on your mind.
sections.output: A complete Brain Dump of everything currently on your mind

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
An **open loop** is anything you have noticed but not finished or put somewhere safe. "Must reply to Ayanda." "Need to book the car service." "Should look into that course." Each one sits in the background, and your mind keeps checking on it so you don't forget.

That checking has a cost. It interrupts focus at random moments. It shows up at 2am. It makes everything feel urgent at once, because your head has no way to sort the loops. It just knows there are a lot of them.

Capture solves this in a simple way: **write it down somewhere you trust**. Once a loop is captured in a place you know you will look again, your mind can let go of holding it. You no longer need to remember it. You only need to remember to check your list.

Two things make capture work:

- **It must be fast.** If capturing takes longer than ten seconds, you will skip it.
- **It must be trusted.** If you don't look at your list, your brain will go back to holding everything.

The first step is a full **brain dump**: getting every open loop out at once. It often feels messy and long. That is normal. You are not organising yet. You are emptying.

Many people feel lighter just from seeing everything on one page, even before anything is done.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kagiso set a timer for 10 minutes and wrote without stopping. His list had 43 items, including:

- Renew driver's licence
- Reply to the school about the trip
- Idea: start a podcast
- Buy printer ink
- Ask Neo about the invoice
- Fix the leaking tap
- Read the contract before Friday

Nothing was in order. Some were tiny, some were huge. But for the first time he could see the full picture, and he realised half the items were quick jobs he had been carrying around for weeks.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Do the brain dump now. Open your Brain Dump worksheet.

1. Set a timer for **10 minutes**.
2. Write everything on your mind: tasks, worries about things to do, ideas, errands, messages to send, things to buy.
3. Use the prompts on the worksheet if you get stuck: work, home, people, money and admin, errands, health appointments, ideas.
4. Do not organise, judge or skip anything. Messy is fine.

When the timer ends, count your items.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep a fast capture tool with you this week. This can be a notes app on your phone home screen, a small notebook, or voice notes to yourself. Whenever a new loop appears, capture it in under ten seconds.

Each evening, glance at what you captured. You will sort it properly in the next two lessons.

questions.q: What is an open loop?
options: Something noticed but not finished or stored somewhere trusted
questions.explain: Open loops are unfinished things your mind keeps holding on to because they are not stored anywhere safe.

questions.q: During a brain dump, what should you do?
options: Sort each item as you write it
questions.explain: Capture first, organise later. Sorting while dumping slows you down and makes you skip things.

sections.markdown:
- You understand why open loops drain attention.
- You know capture must be fast and trusted.
- You have completed a 10-minute brain dump.

lessons.title: What Belongs in Your Capture System
lessons.summary: The nine kinds of things worth capturing, and why you capture first and organise later.

sections.what: A guide to what belongs in your capture system, from tasks and appointments to questions and things to buy.
sections.why: If you only capture tasks, ideas and commitments still leak back into your head. A wide net makes the system trustworthy.
sections.do: Check your brain dump against the nine capture types and add anything missing.
sections.output: A fuller brain dump with nothing important left out

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your capture system is not just a to-do list. It is the place for **anything that needs your attention later**. Capture all of these:

- **Tasks**: single things to do. "Pay the water bill."
- **Ideas**: things you might want to explore. "Monthly newsletter for clients?"
- **Appointments**: things fixed to a date and time. "Dentist, 14th, 10am."
- **Commitments**: promises you made to others. "Told Mpho I'd send the photos."
- **Questions**: things you need to find out. "Does the warranty cover this?"
- **Things to buy**: shopping and supplies.
- **Projects**: bigger outcomes with several steps. "Move house."
- **Follow-ups**: things you are waiting on or need to chase.
- **Important information**: details you will need again. A reference number, an address, a password hint (never a full password).

One rule matters most: **do not immediately organise everything. Capture first.**

Organising while capturing is slow. It forces a decision on every item, and decisions are exactly where friction lives. Capturing is quick. Organising happens later, in one batch, when you choose to do it.

Commitments and follow-ups are the most commonly missed. They live in conversations, emails and chats, so they never feel like "tasks". Yet they are often the things that cause the most stress when forgotten.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lindiwe checked her brain dump against the nine types. She had plenty of tasks but had missed:

- **Commitments**: "Said I'd help my sister with her CV."
- **Follow-ups**: "Waiting for the landlord to confirm the inspection date."
- **Questions**: "Is the course refund still possible?"
- **Important information**: "Medical aid reference number for the claim."

Adding these four took two minutes and removed four things she had been quietly worrying about.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Go back to your Brain Dump.

1. Read through the nine types: tasks, ideas, appointments, commitments, questions, things to buy, projects, follow-ups, important information.
2. For each type, ask "Is anything of this kind still in my head?"
3. Add anything new. Scan your recent messages and emails for commitments and follow-ups.

Don't sort or tidy yet. Just make the list complete.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, after every conversation or meeting where you agree to something, capture it straight away. "I'll send that tomorrow" becomes an item in your capture tool before you move on.

Try saying "Let me note that" out loud. It buys you the ten seconds you need and signals that you take the promise seriously.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in your capture system?
options: Tasks, ideas, commitments, questions and follow-ups
questions.explain: A trusted capture system holds anything that needs attention later, not just urgent tasks.

questions.q: Why capture first and organise later?
options: Deciding where each item goes slows capture and adds friction
questions.explain: Every decision during capture slows you down. Batch the organising for later.

sections.markdown:
- You know the nine kinds of things worth capturing.
- You have checked your brain dump for missing commitments and follow-ups.
- You know to capture first and organise later.

lessons.title: Build Your Master Capture List
lessons.summary: Combine everything into one list and classify each item into one of seven types.

sections.what: A single Master Capture List holding everything on your mind, with each item labelled by type.
sections.why: One list means one place to look. Classifying each item tells you what to do with it next.
sections.do: Move every brain-dump item into your Master Capture List and classify it.
sections.output: Your Master Capture List

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Now you turn the brain dump into a working list. Start by putting everything in **one place**. Not three apps and a notebook. One. If you already have items scattered across sticky notes, emails and apps, bring them in too.

Then classify each item as one of seven types:

- **Task**: a single action you can do. "Buy printer ink."
- **Project**: needs more than one step. "Plan the birthday party." You will break these down in Module 4.
- **Appointment**: tied to a date or time. Put it in your calendar too.
- **Idea**: interesting, but not a commitment yet.
- **Reference**: information to keep, not act on.
- **Waiting**: someone else needs to act first. Note who and since when.
- **Someday**: you might do it, but not now. Parking it is a decision, not a failure.

Classifying is fast if you don't overthink it. Ask: "Is this something I do, something I keep, or something I wait for?" Then pick the closest type.

Once classified, your list stops being a wall of noise. Tasks are ready to prioritise. Projects are flagged for breaking down. Ideas and Someday items stop competing with this week's real work.

Choose a home for your list and keep it there. Paper, a notes app or the table in this course all work. What matters is that you know exactly where it is.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kagiso classified his 43 items:

- "Renew driver's licence" became a **Project** (check documents, book slot, go).
- "Buy printer ink" became a **Task**.
- "Dentist on the 14th" became an **Appointment**.
- "Start a podcast" became an **Idea**.
- "Neo to confirm invoice" became **Waiting**.
- "Learn guitar" became **Someday**.
- "Car licence disc number" became **Reference**.

In the end he had 19 tasks, 6 projects, 3 appointments, and 15 items that no longer needed attention this week.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Master Capture List.

1. Add every item from your Brain Dump as a row.
2. Use the type column to classify each one. Don't spend more than 10 seconds per item.
3. For Waiting items, note who you are waiting on.
4. Add any Appointments to your calendar as well.

Count your Tasks and Projects. Those move into Module 3.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Make this your one capture home. For the rest of the week, every new item goes here, either directly or via your quick capture tool, which you empty into the list once a day.

Pick a daily moment to process new items, such as after lunch or before closing your laptop. Five minutes is enough to classify what came in.

questions.q: A friend needs to send you a document before you can finish a task. How do you classify it?
questions.explain: If someone else must act first, it's Waiting. Note who and since when so you can follow up.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of classifying captured items?
options: It shows what needs action now and what can safely wait
It replaces the need for a calendar
It removes the need to review
questions.explain: Classifying separates real tasks from ideas, reference and someday items, so they stop competing for attention.

sections.markdown:
- All your captured items live in one list.
- Every item has one of seven types.
- Appointments are in your calendar.
- You have a daily moment to process new items.

modules.title: Prioritize What Matters
modules.summary: You turn a long list into a realistic set of priorities. You learn to tell what matters from what just feels loud.

lessons.title: Not Everything Is a Priority
lessons.summary: Sort tasks into Must, Should, Could and Not now.

sections.what: A simple way to sort tasks into four categories: Must, Should, Could and Not now.
sections.why: When everything feels important, nothing gets real attention. Four categories make the trade-offs visible.
sections.do: Sort every task on your Master Capture List into one of the four categories.
sections.output: A Priority Matrix with your tasks sorted

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A priority is not simply something important. It is something that **deserves attention relative to the other choices available right now**. That means priorities are always a comparison. If you have 30 "top priorities", you actually have none.

Use four categories:

- **Must**: real consequences if not done soon. A deadline, a promise, a bill.
- **Should**: important and worth doing this week, but the world does not end if it slips a few days.
- **Could**: nice to do, useful, but optional.
- **Not now**: deliberately parked. Not deleted, not forgotten, just not this week.

Two guidelines help:

1. **Keep Must small.** If more than about five items land in Must, check each one. Ask: "What actually happens if this waits a week?" Often the honest answer moves it to Should.
2. **Use Not now generously.** Moving something to Not now is a decision, not a failure. It gives you permission to stop thinking about it.

Many people find the sorting itself brings relief. A list of 30 tasks becomes 4 Musts, 7 Shoulds, 8 Coulds and 11 Not nows. Suddenly the week looks possible.

You will revisit these categories regularly. A Should can become a Must as a deadline approaches. A Not now can come back when you have room.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Naledi had 24 tasks. Her first pass put 14 in Must. She asked "What happens if this waits a week?" for each one.

- "Submit tax documents to accountant" (due Friday): stayed **Must**.
- "Reorganise photo folders": moved to **Not now**.
- "Update CV": moved to **Should**.
- "Try a new recipe": moved to **Could**.

She ended with 4 Musts. For the first time in weeks she knew what Monday was for.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Priority Matrix.

1. Add each Task (and any Project you want to move this week) from your Master Capture List.
2. Choose Must, Should, Could or Not now for each.
3. If you have more than five Musts, ask "What happens if this waits a week?" and move items down where you can.

Aim for 10 minutes, not perfection.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Each morning this week, look only at your Musts first. Choose one to start with. When Musts are moving, look at Shoulds.

If something new arrives, give it a category straight away instead of letting it jump the queue by default.

questions.q: You have 15 tasks marked Must. What is the best next step?
options: Ask what happens if each waits a week and move some down
questions.explain: A Must list that long usually hides Shoulds. Testing each one against real consequences keeps Must small and realistic.

questions.q: What does moving a task to Not now mean?
options: You deliberately parked it so it stops competing for attention
questions.explain: Not now is an active decision. The task is kept, just not this week.

sections.markdown:
- You know the four priority categories.
- Your tasks are sorted in your Priority Matrix.
- Your Must list is small enough to be realistic.

lessons.title: Priority Signals
lessons.summary: Seven signals that help you judge what deserves attention, and why urgent isn't the same as important.

sections.what: Seven signals that help you decide what deserves attention: deadline, consequence, importance, opportunity, effort, energy and dependency.
sections.why: Without clear signals, the loudest or most recent task wins. Signals help you choose on purpose.
sections.do: Use the signals to check and adjust the categories in your Priority Matrix.
sections.output: A Priority Matrix checked against real signals

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
When you are unsure where a task belongs, look at its signals:

- **Deadline**: Is there a real date? Who set it?
- **Consequence**: What actually happens if it is late or not done?
- **Importance**: Does it move something you care about forward: your work, health, family, money, goals?
- **Opportunity**: Is there a window that will close? An offer, an event, a person available now?
- **Effort**: Is it a five-minute job or a full day?
- **Energy**: What kind of energy does it need? Sharp thinking, or simple routine?
- **Dependency**: Is someone waiting on you? Does another task depend on this one?

You do not need to score every signal for every task. Use them when a decision feels stuck.

The most important lesson: **do not confuse urgency with importance.** Urgent things shout. A ringing phone, a new message, a notification. They feel like they need you now. Important things are often quiet: planning, writing, health, relationships. They rarely demand attention until they become a crisis.

If your days are full of urgent-but-unimportant tasks, important work keeps sliding. A useful habit is to ask, "Is this urgent, important, both, or neither?" before reacting.

Dependency deserves special mention. A small task that unblocks someone else, or unlocks a bigger task, often deserves to be done early even if it looks minor.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Bongani was unsure about two Should tasks.

**"Send Zanele the figures"**: 10 minutes of effort, no fixed deadline. But dependency: Zanele cannot finish her report without them. He moved it to **Must** and did it first.

**"Reply to the group chat about the weekend"**: felt urgent because messages kept coming. Low consequence, low importance. He moved it to **Could** and replied that evening.

Two signals changed both decisions in under a minute.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Look at your Priority Matrix.

1. Pick three tasks you felt unsure about.
2. For each, check the seven signals. Note the strongest one in the notes column.
3. Ask "Is this urgent, important, both or neither?"
4. Change its category if the signals suggest it.

Notice whether any small task is blocking someone else.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, before reacting to a new request or message, pause for three seconds and ask: "Urgent, important, both or neither?"

If it is neither, capture it and return to what you were doing. If it is a dependency for someone else, consider doing it early. Small unblockers often have a big impact.

questions.q: Which statement about urgency and importance is true?
options: Urgent tasks demand attention now, but are not always important
questions.explain: Urgency is about timing and noise. Importance is about real value. Mixing them up lets loud tasks crowd out meaningful ones.

questions.q: A 10-minute task is blocking a colleague's work. Which signal makes it worth doing early?
questions.explain: Dependency: others are waiting on you, so a small effort unlocks a lot.

sections.markdown:
- You know the seven priority signals.
- You can tell urgent from important.
- You have adjusted unsure items in your Priority Matrix.

lessons.title: Create Your Weekly Priority List
lessons.summary: Choose 1–3 major outcomes for the week, plus supporting, optional and deferred tasks.

sections.what: A short weekly list built around 1–3 major outcomes, with supporting tasks, optional tasks and things you deliberately defer.
sections.why: A week with one to three clear outcomes is far easier to act on than a week with forty tasks.
sections.do: Fill in your Weekly Priority Planner and cut your list to the smallest version that still represents what matters.
sections.output: Your Weekly Priority List

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your Priority Matrix shows everything. Your **Weekly Priority List** shows what this week is actually about. It has four parts:

1. **1–3 major outcomes.** Results, not activities. "Proposal sent to client" rather than "work on proposal". If you only achieved these, the week would still count.
2. **Supporting tasks.** The specific tasks that move those outcomes forward.
3. **Optional tasks.** Useful if there is time. Your Coulds live here.
4. **Things deliberately deferred.** Items you have consciously chosen not to do this week.

Why only one to three outcomes? Because weeks are full of interruptions, appointments and surprises. Three outcomes is ambitious for many weeks. On a heavy week, one is plenty.

The deferred section matters more than it looks. Writing "Not this week: redo website, sort garage" gives your mind permission to stop raising those items. It turns guilt into a decision.

**The challenge:** take your current task list and reduce it to the smallest list that still represents what matters. Not the shortest list you can tolerate. The smallest list that still covers what is truly important this week.

A good test: show the list to yourself on Friday. Would achieving it make the week feel successful? If yes, it is the right list.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Ayanda's Weekly Priority List:

**Major outcomes**
1. Quarterly report submitted.
2. Car booked for service.

**Supporting tasks:** Collect sales figures. Draft summary section. Ask Thabo for the chart. Call the garage.

**Optional:** Reply to the newsletter request. Tidy downloads folder.

**Deferred:** Website redesign. Photo album. New budgeting app.

Her full list had 31 items. This one had 11. On Friday, both outcomes were done.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Weekly Priority Planner.

1. Write the week's date.
2. Choose **1–3 major outcomes**, written as results.
3. List the supporting tasks for each outcome.
4. Add optional tasks.
5. List what you are deliberately deferring.
6. Complete the challenge: cross out anything that does not need to be there.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Put your Weekly Priority List where you will see it every morning. Before starting work each day, ask: "Which supporting task moves an outcome forward today?"

At the end of the week, check your outcomes. If you missed one, don't treat it as failure. Ask what got in the way. That answer goes into next week's plan and your weekly reset later in the course.

questions.q: Which is a well-written major outcome for the week?
questions.explain: Outcomes describe a finished result you can check, not an activity.

questions.q: Why list things you are deliberately deferring?
options: It turns background guilt into a conscious decision
So you remember to feel bad
questions.explain: Naming what you are not doing gives your mind permission to let those items rest this week.

sections.markdown:
- You have chosen 1–3 major outcomes for the week.
- You have listed supporting, optional and deferred tasks.
- You have reduced your list to the smallest version that still matters.
- Your Weekly Priority List is ready.

modules.title: Turn Tasks Into Actions
modules.summary: You turn vague tasks and big projects into clear, physical next actions. When you know exactly what to do, starting gets much easier.
modules.outcome: Your Next-Action System and Next-Action List

lessons.title: Tasks vs Projects
lessons.summary: Spot the difference between a project and an action so nothing stays stuck.

sections.what: The difference between a project, which produces an outcome over several steps, and an action, which you can do right now.
sections.why: Many tasks feel impossible to start because they are really projects in disguise.
sections.do: Find the hidden projects on your Weekly Priority List.
sections.output: A list of the hidden projects on your priority list

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Look at this list:

- Launch my business
- Sort out finances
- Plan Dad's birthday
- Email the plumber

Only one of these is an action. The first three are **projects**: they produce an outcome, but they need several steps. You can't "do" a project. You can only do the next step of it.

"Launch my business" is a project.

"Open the domain registrar and compare three domain names" is an action.

The difference matters because projects written as tasks sit on your list for weeks. Each time you look at them, your mind has to work out where to begin. That extra thinking is friction, and friction is often what makes a task feel heavy.

A simple test: **could you do this in one sitting, without having to decide what to do first?** If yes, it is an action. If no, it is a project.

Projects are not bad. They are just different. They need an outcome and at least one next action. In the next lessons you'll learn to write those actions and break big projects down.

Spotting hidden projects is the first step. Often, just relabelling "Sort out finances" as a project with the action "Download last month's bank statement" is enough to get it moving.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Nomsa checked her Weekly Priority List:

- "Finish presentation" was a **project** (needs outline, slides, rehearsal).
- "Call the clinic to move my appointment" was an **action**.
- "Organise the spare room" was a **project**.
- "Buy bin bags" was an **action**.
- "Get fit" was not even a project. It was a goal, too broad to act on.

She marked the projects for the breakdown worksheet in Lesson 3.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Take your Weekly Priority List and supporting tasks.

1. For each item, ask: "Could I do this in one sitting without deciding what to do first?"
2. Mark each one as Action or Project.
3. For each project, write its outcome: what "done" looks like.

Add your hardest-looking projects to the Task Breakdown Worksheet as rows. You will complete them in Lesson 3.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, when you write anything new on your list, check it. If it is a project, add "(project)" next to it and write one next action underneath.

Don't let project-sized items sit on your list pretending to be tasks. That is often why a list feels heavier than it should.

questions.q: Which is an action rather than a project?
options: Email the plumber to ask for a quote
questions.explain: It can be done in one sitting with no further decisions. The others need several steps.

questions.q: What is a quick test for whether something is a project?
options: It takes more than a day
You can't do it in one sitting without first deciding what to do
questions.explain: If you would have to stop and work out the first step, it's a project with hidden steps.

sections.markdown:
- You can tell a project from an action.
- You have marked the projects hidden on your priority list.
- You have written what "done" looks like for each project.

lessons.title: The Next Action Rule
lessons.summary: Write next actions as Verb + object + clear finish so you always know how to start.

sections.what: A simple rule for writing next actions: Verb + object + clear finish.
sections.why: If you don't know how to start, the task usually isn't specific enough. A well-written action removes that guesswork.
sections.do: Rewrite your vague tasks as next actions using the formula.
sections.output: A set of clear next actions for your current tasks

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The Next Action Rule is simple:

> If you do not know how to start, the task is probably not specific enough.

Fix it with this formula:

**Verb + object + clear finish**

- **Verb**: a physical or digital action. Open, write, email, call, draft, list, book, send.
- **Object**: the specific thing. The proposal, Sarah, the March spreadsheet.
- **Clear finish**: how you know you're done. First paragraph drafted. Quote sent. Expenses entered.

Examples:

- Draft the first paragraph of the proposal.
- Email Sarah the revised quote.
- Open the spreadsheet and enter March expenses.

Notice what the verbs are not: "think about", "work on", "deal with", "sort out". These are vague verbs. They don't tell your hands what to do.

The clear finish matters too. "Write proposal" has no end in sight. "Draft the first paragraph" has a finish line you can reach today. Reaching a finish line builds momentum.

A good next action is often smaller than feels necessary. That is a feature. If you can picture yourself doing it, you are far more likely to start.

If writing the action still feels hard, that is a sign there is a hidden step first, like finding a document or asking someone a question. Make that the next action instead.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Vague tasks, rewritten:

- "Sort out insurance" became **"Call the insurer and ask for the claim reference number."**
- "Work on CV" became **"Open my CV and update the latest job title and dates."**
- "Deal with emails" became **"Reply to the three emails flagged yesterday."**
- "Plan trip" became **"List three possible dates and send them to the family group."**

Each one has a verb you can picture, a specific object and a finish line.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Next Action Generator.

1. Choose one vague task from your Weekly Priority List.
2. Fill in the verb, the object and the clear finish.
3. Write the full next action as one sentence.
4. Ask: "Can I picture myself doing this?" If not, make it smaller.

Repeat for at least three tasks. Add the finished actions to your Next-Action List.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the rest of this week, before you close your list for the day, check that every item on tomorrow's list starts with a clear verb. Replace any "work on" or "sort out" with a real action.

Use the Next Action Generator whenever a task has been sitting untouched for more than two days. That is usually a sign it isn't specific enough yet.

questions.q: Which is a well-written next action?
options: Open the budget spreadsheet and enter this week's grocery costs
questions.explain: It has a clear verb, a specific object and a visible finish line.

questions.q: You can't picture yourself doing a next action. What should you do?
options: Make it smaller or find the hidden first step
questions.explain: If you can't picture it, there is a hidden step or it's too big. Shrink it until starting is obvious.

sections.markdown:
- You know the Verb + object + clear finish formula.
- You have rewritten at least three vague tasks as next actions.
- Your Next-Action List has started.

lessons.title: Break Down Overwhelming Tasks
lessons.summary: Use Outcome → Milestone → Task → Next Action to make big work feel possible.

sections.what: A breakdown method that turns overwhelming work into steps: Outcome → Milestone → Task → Next Action.
sections.why: Big tasks feel overwhelming because the whole thing lands on you at once. Breaking them down gives you one visible step at a time.
sections.do: Complete the Task Breakdown Worksheet for five difficult tasks.
sections.output: Your Next-Action List built from five broken-down tasks

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
When a task feels overwhelming, break it down in four layers:

**Outcome → Milestone → Task → Next Action**

- **Outcome**: what done looks like. "Spare room ready for guests."
- **Milestone**: a meaningful checkpoint. "Clutter cleared." "Bed set up."
- **Task**: work that moves a milestone forward. "Sort the boxes."
- **Next action**: the very first physical step. "Carry the three boxes by the door to the lounge."

You don't need to plan every task in advance. You only need the outcome, a rough set of milestones, and one clear next action. When that action is done, you write the next one.

The worksheet asks six questions for each difficult task:

1. **Desired outcome**: what does finished look like?
2. **Why it matters**: the reason, in a sentence. This helps on low-motivation days.
3. **First physical or digital action**: using Verb + object + clear finish.
4. **Estimated effort**: a rough guess. Ten minutes? Two hours? A few sessions?
5. **Possible blocker**: what might stop you? A missing document, a question, a feeling?
6. **Smaller version**: what is a lighter version you could do on a hard day?

The smaller version is your safety net. On a low-energy day, "write the full report" might be too much, but "write three bullet points" is still progress. Progress on hard days keeps the task alive.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Thabo's difficult task: "Apply for the new role."

- **Desired outcome:** Application submitted before the 30th.
- **Why it matters:** Better hours and closer to home.
- **First action:** Open the job advert and copy the requirements into a document.
- **Estimated effort:** About three sessions of an hour.
- **Possible blocker:** Not sure which referees to use.
- **Smaller version:** Write two sentences about why I want the role.

He turned the blocker into its own next action: "Message Lindi to ask if she'll be a referee."

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Task Breakdown Worksheet.

1. Choose **five difficult tasks**, the ones you have been avoiding or that feel too big.
2. For each, complete all six columns.
3. If a blocker appears, write a next action to remove it.
4. Copy every first action into your Next-Action List.

Spend about two to three minutes per task. Rough is fine.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Your Next-Action List is now your main working list. Each day, pick from it rather than from your full capture list.

When you finish an action, write the next one for that task straight away while the context is fresh. If a task stalls for several days, use its smaller version to keep it moving.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the breakdown method?
questions.explain: Start with what done looks like, then checkpoints, then tasks, then the very first step.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the smaller version of a task?
options: To keep making progress on low-energy or difficult days
questions.explain: A smaller version keeps the task moving when the full step feels like too much.

sections.markdown:
- You know the Outcome → Milestone → Task → Next Action method.
- You have broken down five difficult tasks.
- You have a smaller version and blocker plan for each.
- Your Next-Action List is ready to use.

modules.title: Start Tasks
modules.summary: You learn to treat starting as a skill of its own. You build a simple, repeatable way to get from deciding to doing.
modules.outcome: Your Start Now system and Start Now Decision Card

lessons.title: Starting Is Its Own Skill
lessons.summary: Why you don't need to feel ready, and how to shrink the gap between deciding and doing.

sections.what: A new way of seeing task initiation: starting is a separate skill from doing the task well.
sections.why: Waiting to feel ready often means waiting a long time. Treating starting as a skill gives you something you can practise.
sections.do: Notice where your decide-to-do gap is widest and name what fills it.
sections.output: A clear picture of what sits between deciding and starting for you

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Many people believe they need to feel motivated, focused or ready before they can begin. So they wait. They tidy, check messages, make coffee, and wait some more.

Here's the shift: **you do not need to feel ready before beginning.** For many people, readiness shows up after starting, not before.

Starting is its own skill. It's separate from being good at the task. You can be excellent at writing reports and still find it very hard to open the document. That doesn't mean you're lazy. It means the starting part needs its own support.

The aim is to **reduce the distance between deciding and doing.** That distance is usually filled with things like:

- Not knowing the first step.
- Having to find files, tools or information first.
- A task that feels too big or unclear.
- A feeling about the task: boredom, dread, worry about doing it badly.
- Too many other things competing for attention.

You've already handled some of these. Module 4 made first steps clear. Module 3 made priorities clear. This module tackles the rest: shrinking the commitment, removing setup friction, and using outside structure.

Think of it like the first push on a bicycle. The first metre takes the most effort. After that, momentum helps you.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Zinhle decides at 9am to write a client update. She starts at 11:30. In between: she checks email "first", realises she needs last week's numbers, can't find the file, gets distracted by a message, then feels too behind to start.

When she looked at the gap, the fillers were clear: unclear first step, missing file, and a pile-up feeling. None of it was about the update itself. It was all starting friction.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Look back at your Personal Productivity Profile, especially your "tasks you avoid" list.

1. Pick one avoided task.
2. Think about the last time you meant to start it. What happened between deciding and doing?
3. Write down what filled the gap. Use the list in this lesson as prompts.
4. Circle the filler that shows up most often.

You'll design around it in the next three lessons.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
This week, when you notice yourself waiting to feel ready, say to yourself: "I don't need to feel ready. I just need to start."

Then do the smallest possible first step, even just opening the file. Notice what happens to your readiness after a minute or two. Add what you notice to your profile.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does readiness often appear?
questions.explain: For many people, readiness and momentum build once they are already moving.

questions.q: Which of these commonly fills the gap between deciding and doing?
options: Having to find files or information first
questions.explain: Setup tasks like hunting for files are classic starting friction. The others make starting easier.

sections.markdown:
- You know starting is a separate skill from doing the task.
- You have looked at what fills your decide-to-do gap.
- You know your most common starting blocker.

lessons.title: The Five-Minute Start
lessons.summary: Commit to just five minutes to cross the starting threshold.

sections.what: A low-pressure technique: commit to working on a task for just five minutes.
sections.why: Committing to the whole task can feel huge. Five minutes is small enough to say yes to.
sections.do: Use a five-minute start on one task you have been avoiding.
sections.output: One avoided task actually started

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The Five-Minute Start is simple: **commit to beginning for five minutes.** That's it.

The objective is **not to finish**. It's to cross the starting threshold. Once you're past it, you can choose what to do next:

- Keep going, because it turned out easier than expected.
- Stop, because five minutes was the deal.
- Set another five minutes.

All three are valid. Stopping after five minutes is a success, not a failure. You started, and the task now has some progress. Next time it'll feel less heavy because it's no longer untouched.

Why does this work for many people? Because the brain compares effort to reward. "Write the whole report" feels like a lot of effort. "Write for five minutes" feels manageable, so resistance drops.

A few tips:

- **Pair it with a clear next action** from Module 4. "Five minutes on the report" is vague. "Five minutes drafting the opening paragraph" is clear.
- **Use a visible timer.** A phone timer, kitchen timer or clock on screen makes the commitment real.
- **Keep the promise to yourself.** If you said you could stop at five minutes, allow it. That keeps the technique trustworthy next time.

If five minutes still feels like too much, use two. The number doesn't matter. Crossing the threshold does.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Mandla had avoided his tax paperwork for three weeks. He set a five-minute timer with one action: "Put all tax documents into one folder."

At five minutes, he had gathered most of them. He felt the task was smaller than he'd feared, so he set another ten minutes and listed what was missing.

The next day, he didn't need the trick at all. The task was already moving.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Choose one task from your Next-Action List that you've been avoiding.

1. Write its next action clearly.
2. Set a timer for five minutes.
3. Start the action. Nothing else.
4. When the timer ends, choose: continue, stop, or another five minutes.
5. Note how it felt before and after.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Use the Five-Minute Start at least once a day this week, ideally on your hardest Must.

Notice which tasks you continue past five minutes. That's useful data: those tasks were mainly blocked at the starting point, not by the work itself.

questions.q: What is the objective of the Five-Minute Start?
options: To finish the task in five minutes
questions.explain: The aim is getting started. Finishing is not required.

questions.q: You stop after five minutes as agreed. What does that mean?
options: You succeeded: you started and made progress
The technique doesn't work for you
questions.explain: Keeping the deal makes the technique trustworthy and the task now has momentum.

sections.markdown:
- You know how to use the Five-Minute Start.
- You have started at least one avoided task.
- You know stopping after five minutes still counts.

lessons.title: Remove Starting Friction
lessons.summary: Six small setup steps that make it easier to begin.

sections.what: A short pre-start routine that removes small barriers before you begin a task.
sections.why: Small setup tasks like finding a file can quietly stop you. Clearing them first makes starting far easier.
sections.do: Run the six-step pre-start routine on your next task and fill in your Start Now Card.
sections.output: A completed Start Now Card for your next task

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A lot of starting friction is tiny. Each obstacle on its own looks trivial, but together they add up to "I'll do it later". Clear them before you start:

1. **Open the required file.** Have the document, spreadsheet or page already on screen.
2. **Put materials within reach.** Notebook, charger, papers, water.
3. **Close irrelevant tabs.** Each open tab is an invitation to wander.
4. **Silence unnecessary notifications.** Phone on silent or in another room; turn off desktop pop-ups.
5. **Decide the first action.** Use your Verb + object + clear finish.
6. **Set a short focus period.** Five, fifteen or twenty-five minutes. Choose what feels doable.

You can even do the setup the night before. Leaving the file open on your laptop, or putting the forms on the table, turns tomorrow's start into a single step.

The Start Now Card brings all of this into five questions:

1. What am I starting?
2. What is the first action?
3. What can I remove from the environment?
4. What is my minimum commitment?
5. What happens immediately after I start?

The last question is easy to miss. Deciding what comes next, such as "After the first paragraph, I'll add the headings", means you don't hit a new wall the moment you finish your first action.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Refilwe's Start Now Card for her monthly report:

1. **Starting:** Monthly sales report.
2. **First action:** Open the template and paste in this month's totals.
3. **Remove:** Phone to the kitchen, close email and news tabs.
4. **Minimum commitment:** 10 minutes.
5. **Immediately after:** Write three bullet points on what changed.

She filled it in the evening before. In the morning, she sat down and the first step was already obvious.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Start Now Card.

1. Choose the next task you need to start, today or tomorrow.
2. Answer all five questions.
3. Do as much of the setup as you can now: open the file, gather materials.
4. When it's time, follow your card.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Use the Start Now Card for your hardest task each day this week. Fill it in at the end of the previous day if you can. It takes two minutes and saves a lot of morning hesitation.

Keep a blank card somewhere visible: printed on your desk or saved on your phone's home screen.

questions.q: Which is part of removing starting friction?
options: Opening the required file before you begin
Keeping all tabs open in case you need them
questions.explain: Having the file already open removes one more step between you and the work.

questions.q: Why does the Start Now Card ask what happens immediately after you start?
options: So you don't stall once the first action is done
questions.explain: Knowing the step after the first one keeps momentum going.

sections.markdown:
- You know the six pre-start setup steps.
- You have completed a Start Now Card.
- You know you can prepare the night before.

lessons.title: Body Doubling and External Cues
lessons.summary: Use other people and visible signals as outside structure for starting.

sections.what: Two ways to borrow structure from outside yourself: working alongside someone (body doubling) and using visible cues to mark the start of work.
sections.why: Some people find it much easier to start when someone else is present or a clear signal says it's time. That support is legitimate, not a crutch.
sections.do: Choose one external cue or body-doubling option and add it to your Start Now Card.
sections.output: Your finished Start Now Decision Card with outside structure built in

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Some people work better when another person is present. This is often called **body doubling**. The other person doesn't help with the task. They just share the time and space.

Options include:

- A friend or colleague working quietly at the same table.
- A video call where both people work with cameras on and microphones off.
- Working in a library, café or shared workspace where others are focused.
- A scheduled co-working session with a friend: "Tuesday 7pm, one hour, we both do admin."

**External cues** are visible signals that mark the beginning of work. They help because they make "now" clear. Examples:

- Putting on a particular playlist or pair of headphones.
- Turning on a desk lamp only used for work.
- A visible timer on your desk.
- Moving to a specific chair or spot.
- A sticky note on your screen with the first action.

The idea is simple: **use external structure where it helps.** If internal motivation is unreliable, borrow structure from the outside. There's nothing weaker about it. Many people who seem very organised rely on deadlines, meetings and colleagues for exactly this reason.

Experiment. Try one cue for a few days. If it helps, keep it. If not, try another. Check your Productivity Profile: "situations where you focus well" often contains clues.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sizwe found admin very hard to start alone. His profile said he focused well "when someone else is working too".

He set up a weekly video call with his cousin, Thursday 6–7pm. Both kept cameras on, said their goal out loud at the start, and shared what they'd done at the end.

He also added a cue: his work playlist only plays during admin time. Within a few weeks, the first song was enough to signal "time to begin".

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Choose one external support to try this week.

1. Check "situations where you focus well" in your profile.
2. Pick either a body-doubling option or a visible cue.
3. Add it to your Start Now Card under "What can I remove from the environment?" or "What is my minimum commitment?", whichever fits.
4. If it involves someone else, send them a message now to set a time.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Use your chosen support at least twice this week. Pair it with your Start Now Card and a Five-Minute Start.

This is your **Start Now system**: card, short commitment, and outside structure. After a week, notice which parts helped most and keep those.

questions.q: What is body doubling?
options: Working alongside another person who shares the time and space
Hiring someone to do your work
questions.explain: The other person doesn't do the work. Their presence provides structure that can make starting easier.

questions.q: Which is an example of an external cue?
options: A specific playlist that only plays during focused work
questions.explain: A consistent, visible or audible signal helps mark the moment work begins.

sections.markdown:
- You know how body doubling and external cues can help.
- You have chosen one outside support to try.
- Your Start Now Decision Card is complete.
- You have a Start Now system: card, short commitment and outside structure.

modules.title: Focus & Distraction
modules.summary: You design your environment and sessions so focus takes less effort. You learn to treat distractions as information, not personal failure.
modules.outcome: Your Focus System and Distraction Log

lessons.title: Design the Environment
lessons.summary: Change what's around you before demanding more concentration from yourself.

sections.what: A look at the seven environmental factors that affect focus, from notifications to unclear tasks.
sections.why: It's usually easier to change your surroundings than to force more concentration. Small changes can remove many distractions before they start.
sections.do: Audit your workspace against the seven factors and make three changes.
sections.output: Three environment changes that make focus easier

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Focus isn't only about effort. It is strongly affected by what's around you. Seven common factors:

- **Notifications**: every ping is an invitation to switch.
- **Open tabs**: each one is a doorway to something else.
- **Phone proximity**: a phone within reach is easy to pick up without thinking.
- **Noise**: conversations, TV, traffic. Some people need quiet; others focus better with background sound.
- **Visual clutter**: piles of papers and objects in view pull attention.
- **Unclear tasks**: if you don't know exactly what to do, your mind looks for something easier.
- **Interruptions**: people dropping by, calls, household needs.

The principle: **change the environment before demanding more concentration.** Telling yourself to "just focus harder" while your phone buzzes beside you is setting yourself up for a struggle.

Simple changes often help:

- Put your phone in another room, or face down out of reach.
- Turn on "do not disturb" for a set time.
- Close every tab not needed for this task.
- Use headphones, with or without sound.
- Clear only the area directly in front of you, not your whole home.
- Let people know your focus time: a sign on the door, a status message.

Notice that unclear tasks are on the list. The next-action work from Module 4 is also focus work. A clear task gives your attention somewhere to land.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Palesa worked from her kitchen table. Her distractions: phone beside her laptop, 14 open tabs, the family walking through.

She made three changes:

1. Phone charges in the bedroom during morning focus time.
2. One browser window for the current task only.
3. Headphones on means "please don't interrupt unless urgent", agreed with her household.

She didn't suddenly become a different person. She just removed three things that had been pulling at her all day.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Look at the place where you usually work.

1. Go through the seven factors one by one.
2. Rate each quickly: is this a problem for me? Use your profile's distraction list.
3. Choose **three changes** you can make today.
4. Write them in the Focus Session Planner notes for your first session.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Make your three changes this week and keep them in place for at least three sessions before judging them.

If one doesn't help, swap it for another. Over time, you'll build a short "focus setup" you can do in under a minute before any important work.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend before demanding more concentration?
questions.explain: Removing distractions from your surroundings is usually easier and more reliable than forcing focus.

questions.q: Why are unclear tasks listed as a focus factor?
options: They aren't really related to focus
Without a clear task, attention looks for something easier
Unclear tasks are always low priority
questions.explain: A clear next action gives your attention somewhere to land.

sections.markdown:
- You know the seven environmental focus factors.
- You have audited your workspace.
- You have chosen three changes to make focus easier.

lessons.title: Single-Tasking
lessons.summary: Choose one defined outcome for each focus session instead of a vague instruction like 'work'.

sections.what: The practice of choosing one defined outcome for each focus session.
sections.why: "Work" is not a task. A single, clear outcome tells you what to do and when you're done.
sections.do: Write one defined outcome for your next three focus sessions.
sections.output: Three clear session outcomes

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A focus session with no clear target tends to drift. You open your laptop to "work", answer an email, glance at a report, check a message, and an hour later you're not sure what you achieved.

Single-tasking means **choosing one defined outcome for a focus session.** Not "work". Not "admin". Not "the project". One specific, finishable result.

Compare:

- Vague: "Work on the website."
- Defined: "Write the text for the About page."

- Vague: "Do admin."
- Defined: "Pay the three bills due this week and file the receipts."

The defined version tells you what to do, what to ignore, and when you're done.

Single-tasking also means **not switching mid-session**. When another task pops into your head, capture it (Module 2) and return to your outcome. Your capture list is what makes single-tasking possible: you don't have to act on the thought or risk losing it.

What if the outcome is too big for one session? Shrink it. "Write the About page" might become "Write the first draft of the About page, rough is fine." What if you finish early? Great. Take a break, review, or choose another defined outcome.

Your next actions from Module 4 make perfect session outcomes. You already wrote them as Verb + object + clear finish.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Busi's afternoon used to be "catch up on stuff". Now she plans:

- **Session 1:** Draft replies to the four client emails flagged this morning.
- **Session 2:** Update the project timeline with the new delivery dates.
- **Session 3:** Book the venue for next month's workshop.

During session 1, she remembered she needed to order stationery. She wrote it on her capture list and went straight back to the emails.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Focus Session Planner.

1. Plan your next three focus sessions.
2. For each one, write **one defined outcome** in the outcome column. Use your Next-Action List.
3. Check each: could you tell, clearly, when it's done?
4. If not, rewrite it until you could.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Every time you start a focus session this week, say or write the outcome first. Keep your capture tool open beside you so any new thought has somewhere to go.

At the end of each session, check: did I complete the outcome? If not, was it too big, or did I switch? Both are useful to know.

questions.q: Which is a well-defined focus session outcome?
options: Write the text for the About page
questions.explain: It's specific and you can tell when it's done.

questions.q: A new task pops into your head mid-session. What should you do?
options: Capture it and return to your outcome
questions.explain: Capturing it frees your mind without breaking focus.

sections.markdown:
- You know what single-tasking means.
- You have defined outcomes for your next three focus sessions.
- You know to capture new thoughts instead of switching.

lessons.title: Focus Sessions
lessons.summary: Build a repeatable focus cycle: Define → Prepare → Focus → Break → Review.

sections.what: A simple, repeatable five-step focus cycle with adjustable session lengths.
sections.why: A repeatable cycle removes decisions. You know how a session begins, runs and ends.
sections.do: Run one full focus session using the cycle and log it in your Focus Session Planner.
sections.output: A completed, reviewed focus session

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A focus session is a short, planned block of attention on one outcome. The cycle has five steps:

**Define → Prepare → Focus → Break → Review**

1. **Define.** Choose your one outcome (Lesson 6.2).
2. **Prepare.** Set up your environment (Lesson 6.1) and remove starting friction (Module 5). Open the file. Phone away.
3. **Focus.** Work on the outcome for a set time. Capture stray thoughts instead of acting on them.
4. **Break.** Step away. Stand, stretch, get water, look outside. Avoid breaks that pull you in, like scrolling, if they make returning hard.
5. **Review.** Ask: Did I reach the outcome? What helped? What got in the way? What's the next outcome?

**Session length should be adjustable, not a universal rule.** You may have heard of 25-minute sessions. That's one option. Some people work best in 10 minutes. Others find 45 or 60 minutes ideal for deep work. Your best length may change with the task and your energy.

Start with a length that feels slightly easy. A session you complete builds confidence. A session you abandon halfway builds resistance. You can always extend.

The review step is what turns sessions into a system. It's two minutes. Over time, your reviews will show you your best session length, your best times of day and your most common interruptions.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Jabu's Focus Session Planner entry:

- **Outcome:** Write the first draft of the funding application summary.
- **Prep:** Template open, phone in drawer, door closed.
- **Planned:** 20 minutes. **Actual:** 30 minutes. He kept going because it flowed.
- **Result:** Done.
- **Review:** Morning worked well. Next time, have the budget figures ready, as hunting for them cost five minutes.

His next session outcome: "Draft the budget section."

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Run one full focus session now or later today.

1. In the Focus Session Planner, write the date and your outcome.
2. Choose a planned length that feels slightly easy.
3. Prepare your environment and tick the prep box.
4. Focus, then take a short break.
5. Fill in actual minutes, result and a one-line review.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Aim for at least one focus session per working day this week. Log each one in the planner. Try at least two different session lengths.

At the end of the week, look at your log. Which lengths and times led to "Done" most often? That's your starting focus rhythm. You'll match it to your energy later in the course.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the focus cycle?
questions.explain: Define the outcome, prepare the space, focus, break, then review.

questions.q: How long should a focus session be?
options: Adjustable, starting with a length that feels slightly easy
questions.explain: There is no universal rule. Start where you can succeed and adjust from what your reviews show.

sections.markdown:
- You know the five-step focus cycle.
- You have run and logged at least one full focus session.
- You know to adjust session length to what works for you.

lessons.title: Distraction Log
lessons.summary: Record distractions without judgment to find patterns you can design around.

sections.what: A simple log of distractions: what happened, what triggered it, what you did, and what could make the next session easier.
sections.why: Distractions are information. Tracking them without judgment shows patterns you can fix through design rather than willpower.
sections.do: Log every distraction during your next few focus sessions.
sections.output: Your Focus System plus a started Distraction Log

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Distractions will happen. The goal isn't to never be distracted. It's to learn from distractions so the next session is easier.

The Distraction Log has four questions:

1. **What happened?** "Picked up my phone." "Started tidying the desk." "Opened a news site."
2. **What triggered it?** A notification? A hard part of the task? Boredom? Hunger? A noise?
3. **What did I do?** "Scrolled for 10 minutes." "Came back after a minute."
4. **What could make the next session easier?** "Phone in another room." "Break the hard part into a smaller step." "Eat before starting."

The most important rule: **record without judging.** "Got distracted again, I'm hopeless" helps nobody. "Opened email when I reached the difficult section" is useful. It suggests the distraction was a way of escaping a hard moment, which a smaller next action might fix.

After a week or so, look for patterns:

- Do most distractions come from your phone? That's an environment fix.
- Do they happen at the hard parts? That's a task-clarity fix.
- Do they cluster at certain times? That might be an energy pattern.

Every pattern points to a design change. Over time, your Focus System becomes your environment setup, single-task outcomes, focus cycle and the fixes your log reveals.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Two entries from Musa's log:

- **What happened:** Opened YouTube. **Trigger:** Got stuck on a formula. **What I did:** Watched two videos (15 min). **Next time:** When stuck, write the question down and move to the next section.
- **What happened:** Checked phone. **Trigger:** Notification sound. **What I did:** Replied to a message, lost my place. **Next time:** Do not disturb on during sessions.

After a week, he saw that most distractions came when he got stuck, not from boredom.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Distraction Log.

1. Keep it open during your next focus session.
2. Each time you notice a distraction, add a row: what happened, the trigger, what you did.
3. After the session, fill in "what could make the next session easier" for each row.

Short notes are fine. Accuracy matters more than detail.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Log distractions for at least three focus sessions this week. At the end of the week, read the log and circle the most common trigger.

Make one design change based on it, such as moving your phone, preparing materials, or shrinking hard steps. Then add that change to your focus setup. This is your Focus System growing from real evidence.

questions.q: What is the most important rule when keeping a Distraction Log?
options: Record every minute of your day
questions.explain: Judgment makes logging unpleasant and hides the useful information. Neutral notes reveal patterns.

questions.q: Your log shows most distractions happen when you hit a difficult part of a task. What is a likely fix?
options: Break the hard part into a smaller, clearer next action
questions.explain: Distractions at hard moments often point to an unclear or oversized step. Shrinking it helps.

sections.markdown:
- You know the four Distraction Log questions.
- You have logged distractions without judgment.
- You have identified at least one pattern and a design change.
- Your Focus System and Distraction Log are in place.

modules.title: Time Blocking & Flexible Scheduling
modules.summary: Give important work a real place in your day with flexible blocks, built-in buffers and a quick way to recover when plans change.

lessons.title: Time Is a Constraint
lessons.summary: See why a list alone isn't a plan, and how to count the time you really have.

sections.what: The difference between a task list and a schedule, and why important work needs a place in your day.
sections.why: A list shows everything that exists, but it never warns you that your day only holds so many usable hours. Without a place in time, important work keeps losing to whatever is loudest.
sections.do: Compare your planned work with the real, usable hours you have tomorrow.
sections.output: A realistic count of your usable hours and a plan that fits them

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A task list tells you what exists. A schedule gives important work a place.

Most lists quietly assume unlimited time. You write down twenty things, and each one looks reasonable on its own. Together they would need three days. The list does not warn you, so at the end of the day it looks like you failed, when really the plan was impossible from the start.

Time is the constraint every plan has to respect. Once you see it, a few things change:

- You stop asking "What do I need to do?" and start asking "What fits today?"
- Important work gets a slot instead of waiting for a free moment that never arrives.
- Unfinished items stop feeling like proof that something is wrong with you. They simply did not fit.

**Usable hours are fewer than total hours.** An eight-hour workday rarely holds eight hours of focused work. Meetings, messages, meals, travel, transitions and small interruptions all take their share. Many people find they have three to five genuinely usable hours, sometimes less.

**Estimates usually run short.** Most of us picture the task going smoothly. Rounding estimates up is not pessimism; it is accuracy.

This is not a reason to plan less ambitiously. It is a reason to plan honestly. When your plan matches your real hours, you choose what matters on purpose instead of by accident.

> A plan that fits is more useful than a plan that impresses.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lerato's list for Thursday has 14 items. She opens her calendar: a 10:00 meeting, a 13:00 call, school pick-up at 15:00. Between them she has roughly four usable hours. She gives each item a rough estimate and finds the list needs about nine.

Instead of starting at the top and hoping, she picks the proposal draft (2 hours) and three quick admin items (1 hour), keeps an hour free for the unexpected, and moves the rest to Friday or back to her weekly list. On Thursday evening everything she planned is done. The list did not shrink because she worked harder. It shrank because she was honest about time.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Take tomorrow, or your next workday.

1. Write down your fixed commitments and their times.
2. Look at the gaps between them. Subtract travel, meals and changeover time. What remains is your usable time.
3. Open your Weekly Priority Planner and pull out the items you hope to do tomorrow. Give each a rough time estimate, and round up.
4. Compare the two numbers. If the work is bigger than the hours, circle what moves to another day.
