Keep these numbers. In the next lesson you will turn them into blocks.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the next three days, do a two-minute check before you start work: how many usable hours do I have, and how many hours of work have I planned? If the plan is bigger, cut before you begin rather than after you fall behind.

Notice how often your original list would have overflowed. That pattern is useful information about how you plan, not a judgement on how you work.

questions.q: What does a schedule give you that a task list does not?
options: A complete record of every task
A place in time for important work
questions.explain: A list shows what exists. A schedule gives the important items an actual place in your day, so they are not left waiting for a free moment.

questions.q: You have about 4 usable hours and 9 hours of planned work. What is the most useful response?
options: Start at the top and work faster
Choose what fits and deliberately move the rest
Skip all breaks so it fits
questions.explain: Choosing what fits, and moving the rest on purpose, keeps the plan honest and protects the work that matters most.

sections.markdown:
- You know the difference between what exists (your list) and what fits (your schedule).
- You counted your real usable hours for a day.
- You compared planned work with available time and decided what moves.

lessons.title: Use Flexible Blocks
lessons.summary: Group your day into a few flexible blocks instead of scheduling every minute.

sections.what: A way to plan your day in a handful of labelled blocks, such as deep work, admin and recovery, rather than minute-by-minute appointments.
sections.why: Minute-by-minute schedules break the moment anything runs late. Blocks give your day shape while leaving room to choose the exact task inside each one.
sections.do: Build tomorrow as 4 to 7 flexible blocks in the Flexible Daily Planner.
sections.output: Your first Flexible Daily Planner

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Instead of scheduling every minute, create blocks. A block is a stretch of time with a purpose, not a promise to do one exact task at one exact second.

Use these block types:

- **Deep work** for focused, demanding work: writing, building, thinking, problem-solving.
- **Admin** for small, necessary tasks: forms, filing, bookings, payments.
- **Communication** for email, messages and calls, batched instead of scattered all day.
- **Errands** for anything that takes you out or around the house.
- **Recovery** for breaks, meals, movement, a walk, a quiet moment. This is part of the plan, not a reward for finishing it.
- **Personal** for family, friends, health appointments, hobbies, life.

**Why blocks work.** A block reduces the number of decisions you make during the day. When the Admin block starts, you do not need to ask "what now?" You open your admin list. A block is also forgiving: if one task takes longer, you have the rest of the block to absorb it.

**Keep blocks few and clear.** Four to seven blocks in a day is plenty. Give your hardest block your best time. Put communication after, not before, your deep work if you can, because inboxes have a way of eating mornings.

**Name one task, not ten.** Each deep work block gets one clear outcome. Admin and communication blocks can hold a short list.

A block plan is a sketch, not a contract. Its job is to make the next action obvious when you look at it.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Sipho's Tuesday in blocks:

- 08:30 to 10:30, Deep work: write the first draft of the training guide.
- 10:30 to 10:45, Recovery: coffee, stretch, no screens.
- 10:45 to 11:30, Communication: reply to client emails, return two calls.
- 11:30 to 12:30, Admin: submit expense claim, book car service.
- 12:30 to 13:30, Personal: lunch with his sister.
- 13:30 to 15:00, Deep work: edit the guide and add examples.
- 15:00 to 16:00, Buffer and wrap-up.

He does not know exactly which email comes first. He does not need to. He knows what each part of the day is for.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Flexible Daily Planner and build tomorrow.

1. Start with fixed commitments. Enter them first.
2. Add one Deep work block in your best-focus time, with one specific task.
3. Add an Admin block and a Communication block. List the few items each holds.
4. Add at least one Recovery block.
5. Leave one block marked Buffer. You will learn why in the next lesson.

Stop at 4 to 7 blocks. If you want more, the day is probably overfull.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Plan in blocks for the next three workdays. Fill the planner the evening before or first thing in the morning, whichever you will actually do. At the end of each day, tick what got done and note which block worked best.

After three days, look for a pattern. Which block type keeps getting squeezed? That is usually the one that needs a firmer place in your day.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a flexible block over a minute-by-minute schedule?
options: It gives the day shape while absorbing overruns and reducing decisions
It removes the need to prioritize
It guarantees every task gets finished
questions.explain: Blocks set a purpose for a stretch of time, so you make fewer moment-to-moment decisions and small overruns do not wreck the whole plan.

questions.q: Where does a Recovery block belong?
options: Only after all work is done
Inside the plan, like any other block
questions.explain: Recovery is part of a workable day. Planning it in makes it more likely to happen and helps the rest of the day run.

sections.markdown:
- You know the seven block types and what each is for.
- You built tomorrow as 4 to 7 flexible blocks.
- Your deep work block has one clear task.

lessons.title: Add Buffers
lessons.summary: Build slack into your day so interruptions and overruns don't sink the plan.

sections.what: Buffers are deliberate gaps in your plan for interruptions, transitions and tasks that run long.
sections.why: Plans fail when there is no room for real life. A buffer turns a small delay into a non-event instead of the start of a collapse.
sections.do: Add buffer time between blocks and one larger buffer block to tomorrow's plan.
sections.output: A daily plan with built-in slack

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Plans fail when there is no room for interruptions, transitions or overruns.

A tightly packed day looks efficient on paper. In practice, one late meeting pushes everything back, the next block starts behind, and by mid-afternoon the plan feels broken. Often the plan was never wrong about the work. It was wrong about the gaps.

Three kinds of buffer help:

1. **Transition buffers.** Five to fifteen minutes between blocks. Switching from one kind of work to another takes time: closing files, getting water, resetting your desk, remembering where you were. Many people who find switching tasks hard notice this most.
2. **Overrun buffers.** Add extra time to tasks you tend to underestimate. A useful starting point is to add half again to your first guess, then adjust as you learn.
3. **A buffer block.** One block in the day, often 30 to 60 minutes, with nothing planned. If the day runs smoothly, use it for a small task from your list or finish early. If it does not, the buffer absorbs the damage.

**Unused buffer is not wasted time.** It is insurance you did not need today. You can always pull a task into it. You cannot pull extra time out of a full day.

**Signs you need more buffer:** you are often late to the next thing, you skip breaks to catch up, or you feel behind before lunch.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Amahle used to plan back-to-back. Her 09:00 call ran ten minutes over, so her 09:30 writing block started late, so she skipped her break, so her 11:00 admin block got pushed to after lunch.

Now she leaves ten minutes after every call and keeps 14:30 to 15:15 open as a buffer block. Last Wednesday the call ran over again. She used the transition time, started writing on schedule and used the buffer block to finish a client form she had been putting off. Same day, same interruptions, very different feeling.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open tomorrow's Flexible Daily Planner.

1. Look at each change from one block to the next. Where you switch type or location, add a 10-minute gap.
2. Find the task you most often underestimate. Increase its time by about half.
3. Add one Buffer block of 30 to 60 minutes, ideally in the afternoon when delays have built up.
4. If everything no longer fits, move the lowest-priority item to another day.

The plan now holds less. That is the point.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep a buffer block every workday this week. At the end of each day, note in the planner what the buffer was used for: an overrun, an interruption, a bonus task or a rest.

By Friday you will have real evidence of how much slack your days need. Adjust the size of your buffer from that evidence, not from how you wish your days went.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a buffer block?
options: To add more tasks to the day
To absorb interruptions and overruns so the plan survives
To punish yourself for falling behind
questions.explain: A buffer gives delays somewhere to go, so one overrun does not knock over the rest of the day.

questions.q: If your buffer goes unused, what does that mean?
options: It was insurance you did not need today
You were not working hard enough
questions.explain: Unused buffer is simply slack you did not need. You can pull a small task into it or finish early.

sections.markdown:
- You know the three kinds of buffer: transition, overrun and a buffer block.
- You added buffers to tomorrow's plan.
- You have a way to learn how much slack your days really need.

lessons.title: Recover From a Broken Plan
lessons.summary: Use a five-step reset to rescue a day that went off track instead of writing it off.

sections.what: A short, repeatable routine for when your day stops going to plan: Stop, Reassess, Keep the most important item, Move lower-priority work, Continue.
sections.why: Many people treat one disrupted plan as a failed day. A quick recovery routine lets you save the part of the day that still matters.
sections.do: Practise the five-step recovery on a real or recent disrupted day.
sections.output: A day-recovery routine and your completed Flexible Daily Planner

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Every plan breaks sometimes. A child gets sick, a client calls with an urgent request, a task turns out twice as big, or your focus is simply not there. The plan is not the problem. The problem is the habit of deciding that once the plan is broken, the day is lost.

When the day changes, use five steps:

1. **Stop.** Pause for a minute. Do not keep pushing through a plan that no longer matches reality.
2. **Reassess.** How much usable time is left? What has changed? What energy do you have?
3. **Keep the most important item.** Pick the one thing that would make today count. If it is too big now, keep a smaller version of it.
4. **Move lower-priority work.** Drag the rest to another day or back to your weekly list. Moving is a decision, not a failure.
5. **Continue.** Start the kept item with its first physical action. Use your Start Now Card if starting feels sticky.

The whole routine takes three to five minutes. It turns a vague sense of "I've lost the day" into a new, smaller plan you can actually do.

**Shrink, do not scrap.** Thirty minutes on the most important task beats a full day of nothing because the original plan felt ruined.

**Expect to use this often.** Recovering well is a skill, and like any skill it gets faster with practice. A system you can restart is worth more than a system you have to follow perfectly.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
At 11:00 Thabo learns a supplier delivery has failed and he must sort it out today. His plan had a deep work block on the quarterly report and an afternoon of admin.

He stops and reassesses: about three usable hours left after the supplier calls. He keeps one item: the report summary page, a smaller version of the full report. He moves the admin to tomorrow's Admin block. He continues by opening the report file and writing the first heading.

By 16:00 the supplier issue is handled and the summary is drafted. The day did not go as planned, but it was not lost.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Think of a recent day that went off track, or use today if it already has.

1. Write down what changed.
2. Estimate the usable time that was (or is) left.
3. Choose the single most important item, or a smaller version of it.
4. List what you would move, and where it would go.
5. Write the first action for the kept item.

Then open your Start Now Card and check: if you had used this routine, what would the rest of that day have looked like?

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Write the five steps somewhere you will see them when a day falls apart: the top of your Flexible Daily Planner, a sticky note, or your phone lock screen. The next time your plan breaks, run the routine before deciding the day is lost.

Use the planner's Buffer and Recovery blocks as places to run it. In the planner, mark moved tasks clearly so nothing gets forgotten.

questions.q: Your plan breaks at midday. What is the third step of the recovery routine?
questions.explain: After stopping and reassessing, you keep the one item that would make today count, or a smaller version of it.

questions.q: What does 'shrink, do not scrap' mean?
options: Keep a smaller version of the key task instead of dropping the day
questions.explain: A smaller version of the most important task still moves you forward, which is better than writing off the whole day.

sections.markdown:
- You have a five-step routine for recovering a broken day.
- You practised it on a real situation.
- Your Flexible Daily Planner now includes blocks, buffers and a recovery plan.

modules.title: Energy-Based Planning
modules.summary: Plan around the energy you actually have, not just the hours on the clock, using task menus and real observation of your patterns.

lessons.title: Match Work to Available Energy
lessons.summary: Sort tasks by the energy they need so you can match work to how you actually feel.

sections.what: A simple way to label tasks as high, medium or low energy, and choose work that fits the energy you have right now.
sections.why: Time alone does not decide what you can do. An hour at your best and an hour when you are drained are not the same hour.
sections.do: Label ten current tasks as high, medium or low energy.
sections.output: An energy-labelled task list

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Most planning treats every hour as equal. It is not. An hour when you are alert and clear-headed can handle work that an hour when you are tired simply cannot. When you ignore this, you end up staring at a demanding task when your energy is low, then feeling guilty for not doing it.

Energy-based planning adds one question to your planning: **how much energy does this task need?**

Use three levels:

- **High energy:** tasks that need sustained thought, creativity or decisions. Starting them is hard and interruptions hurt.
- **Medium energy:** tasks that need attention but have structure. You can do them reasonably well on an ordinary day.
- **Low energy:** tasks that are simple, routine or mechanical. You can do them when tired, distracted or between other things.

**Energy is personal.** A phone call might be low energy for one person and high for another. Label tasks by how they feel to you, not how they look on paper.

**Match, do not force.** When energy is high, protect it for high-energy work. When energy is low, do not stop; switch to something on your low list. Productive low-energy time is still productive.

**Energy is not willpower.** If you notice you cannot start something hard at 16:00, that is information about your energy, not a character flaw. Planning around it is a sensible decision.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Naledi labels her current tasks:

- High: write the funding application, plan the workshop structure.
- Medium: edit last week's newsletter, team check-in meeting, update the project plan.
- Low: file receipts, reply to three short emails, order printer ink, rename photo files.

On Monday afternoon she feels flat after a long meeting. Instead of forcing the application, she clears four low-energy tasks in 40 minutes. On Tuesday morning, with more energy, she starts the application first. Both sessions felt like progress.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open your Master Capture List or your current task list.

1. Pick ten tasks you need to do in the next two weeks.
2. Label each H, M or L based on how it feels to you, not how long it takes.
3. Check the balance. If almost everything is High, look for tasks you can split so part of them becomes Medium or Low.

Keep this labelled list. In the next lesson you will turn it into task menus.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the rest of this week, before you start any block, ask: "What is my energy right now: high, medium or low?" Then choose a task with a matching label.

When you plan tomorrow, add the energy level next to each task. This takes seconds and helps you put high-energy work where you are most likely to manage it.

questions.q: Your energy is low at 15:30. What does energy-based planning suggest?
options: Force yourself through the hardest task
Switch to a task labelled low energy
Feel guilty and try again tomorrow
questions.explain: Matching work to energy means using low-energy time for low-energy tasks, so the time still counts.

questions.q: How should you decide a task's energy level?
options: By how it feels to you personally
questions.explain: Energy needs are personal. The same task can be easy for one person and draining for another.

sections.markdown:
- You know the three energy levels: high, medium and low.
- You labelled ten real tasks by the energy they need.
- You have a quick question to ask before each block: what is my energy right now?

lessons.title: Build Task Menus
lessons.summary: Create ready-made lists of tasks for each energy level so choosing what to do is easy.

sections.what: Task menus are three short lists of work you can pick from: one for high energy, one for medium and one for low.
sections.why: When your energy changes, deciding what to do next can take more effort than the task. A menu removes that decision.
sections.do: Fill in your high, medium and low task menus in the Energy Planner.
sections.output: Your three personal task menus

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
A task menu works like a menu in a restaurant. You do not invent a dish when you are hungry; you choose from options already prepared. When your energy drops, you do not need to think hard about what to do. You look at the right menu and pick.

Typical examples:

- **High energy:** writing, strategy, complex problem-solving, learning something new, difficult conversations.
- **Medium energy:** meetings, editing, planning, reviewing work, structured calls.
- **Low energy:** filing, admin, simple replies, routine tasks, tidying your desk, updating lists.

**Your menu is not your whole task list.** It is a short set of tasks ready to go: clear, specific and startable. Five to eight items per menu is plenty. Write each one as a next action (verb plus object plus clear finish) so it is easy to begin.

**Include "always available" items.** Some tasks are useful any time: clearing downloads, processing your capture list, prepping tomorrow's materials. Put a few on your low-energy menu so there is always something worthwhile when you are tired.

**Include a recovery option.** Sometimes the right choice is a ten-minute walk, a drink of water or a stretch. Recovery is not quitting; it often restores enough energy to move up a menu.

**Refresh weekly.** Menus go stale as tasks get done. Update them during your Weekly Reset.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kagiso's menus, kept at the top of his Energy Planner:

- High: draft section 2 of the business plan; outline the client workshop; solve the pricing spreadsheet error.
- Medium: edit the website About page; plan next week's content; 30-minute call with the accountant.
- Low: file last month's invoices; reply to the three supplier emails; clear the downloads folder; order new chargers.
- Recovery: walk round the block; make tea and sit outside for ten minutes.

When he finishes a meeting feeling drained, he glances at Low and starts on invoices within a minute.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Energy Planner and use your labelled list from the last lesson.

1. Move your High tasks into the high-energy menu, rewriting each as a clear next action.
2. Do the same for Medium and Low.
3. Add two or three "always available" low-energy tasks.
4. Add one or two recovery options that genuinely help you.

Keep each menu short. If one has more than eight items, choose the most important.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Keep your menus where you will see them when your energy shifts: printed beside your desk, pinned in your notes app, or in the planner. This week, every time you finish a block and feel unsure what to do, check your energy and pick from the matching menu without overthinking it.

Cross items off as they are done and add new ones as they come up.

questions.q: Why is a task menu useful when your energy drops?
options: It forces you to do hard tasks
It removes the decision of what to do next
questions.explain: A ready-made menu means you pick from prepared options instead of spending scarce energy deciding.

questions.q: Which belongs on a low-energy menu?
questions.explain: Filing is routine and mechanical, which makes it a good fit for low-energy time.

sections.markdown:
- You have three task menus: high, medium and low energy.
- Each menu item is written as a clear next action.
- You added "always available" tasks and recovery options.

lessons.title: Track Patterns
lessons.summary: Observe your real energy across the day for a week instead of guessing.

sections.what: A short observation habit: noting your energy level at a few points each day so you can see your actual patterns.
sections.why: Many people plan around the energy pattern they think they have. Observation often shows something different, and better plans follow from real data.
sections.do: Log your energy three times a day for seven days, then name your peak and dip windows.
sections.output: Your completed Energy Planner

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Do not assume your energy pattern. Observe it.

You may believe you are a "morning person" or that you "work best under pressure". Those beliefs might be right, or they might be habits you have never tested. Watching for a week often reveals surprises: a reliable slump after lunch, a second wind in the early evening, or a drop on days with lots of meetings.

**How to track.** Three times a day, perhaps mid-morning, early afternoon and late afternoon, note:

- Your energy: high, medium or low.
- What you were doing.
- Anything that might have affected it: sleep, food, a hard meeting, a walk, a noisy space.

This takes under a minute each time. Set phone reminders if it helps.

**What to look for after a week:**

- **Peak window:** when are you most often high? Protect this for deep work.
- **Dip window:** when are you most often low? Put admin, low-energy menu items or recovery here.
- **Boosters and drains:** what tends to come before a high or low? Small changes, like a short walk before a hard task, can make a real difference.

**Patterns are not rules.** A pattern tells you what is likely, not what is guaranteed. Some days will differ. That is why your menus exist.

Tracking is not about judging yourself. It is about gathering the information a good plan needs.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Zanele assumed her best work happened late at night. After a week of tracking, her notes showed high energy most days between 09:00 and 11:30, a steady dip from 14:00 to 15:30, and medium energy in the evening that often dropped after screen-heavy work.

She moved her writing block to 09:30, put email and filing at 14:00, and stopped saving hard tasks for night time. Her evenings became calmer, and her writing got done earlier in the week.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
In the Energy Planner, set up your observation:

1. Choose three check-in times that fit your normal day.
2. Set reminders for them.
3. At each check-in, add a short note: day, time, energy level, what you were doing.

Do a first check-in now so the habit has started. It only needs one line.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Track for seven days. At the end of the week, fill in your peak window, dip window, boosters and drains in the Energy Planner. Then open your Flexible Daily Planner and move your deep work block into your peak window and your admin block into your dip.

Repeat a short tracking week every few months, or whenever your routine changes.

questions.q: Why track energy instead of relying on what you already believe?
options: Beliefs about energy are always wrong
Observation shows your real pattern, which may differ from your assumptions
Tracking is required every day forever
It replaces the need for task menus
questions.explain: Observation gives you real data. It may confirm your beliefs or surprise you, and either way your plans improve.

questions.q: You find your dip window is 14:00 to 15:30. What fits there best?
questions.explain: Putting lower-energy work or recovery in your dip window uses that time well and protects your peak for harder work.

sections.markdown:
- You have a simple way to track energy three times a day.
- You know how to find your peak window, dip window, boosters and drains.
- Your Energy Planner holds your menus and your observed patterns.

modules.title: Projects & Long-Term Goals
modules.summary: Turn big goals into projects with clear next actions, keep only a manageable number active, and track them on one dashboard.
modules.outcome: Your Project-to-Action Map and Project Dashboard

lessons.title: Goal → Project → Milestone → Task → Next Action
lessons.summary: Connect big goals to the one thing you can do today using five clear levels.

sections.what: A five-level map that links a long-term goal all the way down to a single next action you can do now.
sections.why: Big goals feel motivating but are impossible to start directly. The map shows how today's small action connects to the outcome you care about.
sections.do: Take one goal and map it through all five levels to a next action.
sections.output: Your first Goal Planner and Project-to-Action Map

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Big goals often stall for a simple reason: you cannot do a goal. You can only do an action. The five-level map closes that gap.

- **Goal** describes direction. "Become financially more stable." "Build a healthier routine." "Grow my business." Goals are often ongoing and never quite "done".
- **Project** produces an outcome. It has a clear finish line: "Set up a monthly budget", "Launch the new service page", "Run a 5 km event".
- **Milestone** is a meaningful checkpoint inside a project: "Service page draft approved", "Can run 3 km without stopping".
- **Task** moves the project: "Write the service description", "Choose three photos".
- **Next action** tells you what to do now: "Open the website editor and write the first two sentences of the service description."

**Work top-down to plan, bottom-up to act.** When planning, start with the goal and move down. When working, look only at the next action. You do not need to hold the whole project in your head while you work.

**One project at a time per goal, at first.** A goal can produce many projects. Choose the one that would make the most difference now.

**If you are stuck, you are at the wrong level.** Feeling overwhelmed usually means you are trying to act on a goal or project. Drop down a level until the next step is obvious, using the same Verb + object + clear finish rule from Module 4.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Bongani's map:

- Goal: Earn more from my photography.
- Project: Launch a wedding photography package by the end of next month.
- Milestones: 1) Package and price decided. 2) Portfolio page live. 3) First five enquiries answered.
- Tasks for milestone 1: research three local competitors' packages; decide what is included; set a price.
- Next action: Open a new note and list what three competitors include in their wedding packages.

That last line takes twenty minutes. It is the only thing Bongani needs to look at today.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Goal Planner.

1. Write one goal that matters to you right now, and why it matters.
2. List possible projects that would move it forward. Pick one.

Then open the Project-to-Action Map for that project.

3. Write the project outcome as a finished result.
4. Add two to four milestones.
5. List the tasks for the first milestone only.
6. Write the next action for the first task.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Complete the Project-to-Action Map for your chosen project and copy its next action into tomorrow's Flexible Daily Planner. Each time you finish a next action, write the next one immediately while you still remember the context.

Do not map every milestone in detail now. Plan the current milestone fully and keep later ones as short notes.

questions.q: Which of these is a project rather than a goal?
options: Launch the new service page by 30 June
questions.explain: A project has a clear finish line and produces an outcome. The others describe ongoing direction, which makes them goals.

questions.q: You feel stuck and overwhelmed when you think about a goal. What does the map suggest?
options: Drop down a level until the next step is obvious
Work on several projects at once
questions.explain: Being stuck usually means you are trying to act at too high a level. Moving down to a task or next action makes it doable.

sections.markdown:
- You know the five levels: goal, project, milestone, task, next action.
- You chose one goal and one project to move it forward.
- You mapped that project down to a single next action.

lessons.title: Limit Active Projects
lessons.summary: Sort projects into Active, Waiting and Someday so you only juggle what you can handle.

sections.what: A simple way to sort every project into three lists: Active, Waiting and Someday.
sections.why: Too many active projects increase switching and ambiguity. Fewer active projects means each one actually moves.
sections.do: List every project you have and sort each into Active, Waiting or Someday in the Project Planner.
sections.output: A sorted project list with a small, deliberate set of Active projects

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Too many active projects increase switching and ambiguity. Every project you call "active" claims some of your attention, even when you are not working on it. With ten active projects, each gets a sliver of time, progress is slow everywhere, and it becomes hard to tell what to do next.

Sort every project into one of three statuses:

- **Active:** you are working on this now, this week or this month. It has a next action and a place in your plans.
- **Waiting:** progress depends on someone or something else: a reply, an approval, a delivery, a date. Record what you are waiting for and when you will follow up.
- **Someday:** you want to do it, but not now. It is parked on purpose, not forgotten.

**How many Active projects?** There is no universal number, but many people find three to five work-and-personal projects combined is a realistic ceiling. If you are often switching between projects without finishing, try fewer.

**Someday is not failure.** Moving a project to Someday is a clear decision that frees attention. Your Weekly Reset is where you review Someday and promote a project when space opens.

**Waiting needs a follow-up date.** Without one, Waiting quietly turns into forgotten.

**One in, one out.** When a new project wants to become Active and you are at your limit, decide which current project finishes, pauses or moves to Someday.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Refilwe listed eleven projects. Sorted:

- Active (4): client website rebuild; tax paperwork; spare room clear-out; online course for her team.
- Waiting (2): new laptop, waiting for the IT quote, follow up Friday; office lease renewal, waiting for the landlord.
- Someday (5): podcast idea, learning Portuguese, garden redesign, photo album, rewriting her CV.

She felt lighter immediately. Nothing was deleted. Five projects simply stopped pretending to be urgent.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Project Planner.

1. Add every project you can think of, work and personal, one per row. Use your Master Capture List to find them.
2. Give each a status: Active, Waiting or Someday.
3. Count your Active projects. If there are more than you can realistically move this month, move some to Someday.
4. For each Waiting project, write what you are waiting for and when you will follow up in the Blocker column.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Use the Active list as your project filter this week. When something new comes up, capture it, then decide its status before letting it compete for your time. When an Active project finishes, celebrate briefly, then promote one from Someday or Waiting.

Check Waiting follow-up dates every few days so nothing stalls silently.

questions.q: Why limit the number of Active projects?
options: Fewer projects means less work overall
Too many active projects increase switching and make next steps unclear
questions.explain: Each active project claims attention. Fewer active projects mean less switching and clearer progress.

questions.q: What should every Waiting project have?
options: A deadline you set for the other person
A note of what you are waiting for and a follow-up date
questions.explain: Recording what you are waiting for and when you will follow up stops Waiting turning into forgotten.

sections.markdown:
- Every project you have is in one place.
- Each project is marked Active, Waiting or Someday.
- Your Active list is a size you can realistically move.

lessons.title: Project Dashboard
lessons.summary: Set up one dashboard showing each active project's outcome, milestone, next action and blockers.

sections.what: A one-page view of all active projects with the key details for each: outcome, deadline, current milestone, next action, blocker and status.
sections.why: When project details live in your head, every session starts with remembering. A dashboard shows you where each project stands in seconds.
sections.do: Complete the Project Dashboard fields for every Active project.
sections.output: Your Project Dashboard

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
For every active project, record:

- **Outcome:** what "done" looks like, in one sentence.
- **Deadline, if relevant:** a real date only if one exists. Invented deadlines tend to be ignored.
- **Current milestone:** the checkpoint you are working towards now.
- **Next action:** the very next physical or digital step.
- **Blocker:** anything stopping progress, such as missing information, a decision you have not made or a person you need.
- **Status:** Active, Waiting or Someday.

**The next action column is the most important.** If a project has no next action, it will not move. If you cannot write one, the blocker column probably needs filling in, and resolving that blocker becomes your next action.

**Keep it brief.** The dashboard is a map, not a filing cabinet. Detailed notes, files and research belong in the project's folder. One line per field is enough.

**Look at it often.** Glance at the dashboard when planning your day so you can pull next actions into your blocks. Update it fully during your Weekly Reset.

**Blockers are useful signals.** If the same blocker appears week after week, the project may need a decision: ask for help, change the plan, or move it to Someday.

The dashboard answers the question every project eventually raises: "Where was I with this?"

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
One row from Musa's dashboard:

- Project: Family reunion in December.
- Outcome: Venue booked, 40 guests invited, menu confirmed.
- Deadline: invitations out by 15 October.
- Current milestone: Venue booked.
- Next action: Phone the two shortlisted venues to ask about December availability.
- Blocker: Need final budget from his brother.
- Status: Active.

Because the blocker is written down, Musa sends his brother a two-line message that afternoon instead of carrying the worry around.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Project Planner and complete every field for each Active project.

1. Write the outcome as a finished result.
2. Add a deadline only if one is real.
3. Name the current milestone.
4. Write a next action using Verb + object + clear finish.
5. Note any blocker. If there is one, ask whether resolving it should be the next action.

Leave Someday projects brief. They only need a name and status.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Make your Project Dashboard part of your daily planning: before filling your Flexible Daily Planner, glance at the next action column and choose which ones get a block today. When you finish a next action, update the dashboard straight away.

For any project with many steps, keep its full Project-to-Action Map alongside the dashboard.

questions.q: Which dashboard field matters most for keeping a project moving?
questions.explain: Without a next action, a project cannot move. All the other fields support choosing and doing that next step.

questions.q: A project shows the same blocker three weeks in a row. What is a sensible response?
options: Ignore it; it will resolve itself
Make a decision: ask for help, change the plan or move it to Someday
questions.explain: A repeated blocker signals the project needs a decision. Leaving it unchanged keeps it stuck.

sections.markdown:
- You have a Project Dashboard for all Active projects.
- Each Active project has an outcome, current milestone and next action.
- Blockers are visible, so you can act on them.

modules.title: Weekly Reset
modules.summary: Keep your system trustworthy with a short weekly session that clears loose ends, updates projects and rebuilds the week ahead.

lessons.title: Why Reset
lessons.summary: Understand why a regular reset keeps your system trustworthy, and why it isn't a performance review.

sections.what: A weekly reset is a short, regular session where you bring your system back up to date and restore clarity.
sections.why: Every system drifts: lists go stale, notes pile up, plans stop matching reality. Without maintenance, you stop trusting the system and stop using it.
sections.do: Choose a day, time and place for your weekly reset.
sections.output: A scheduled weekly reset slot

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
The system needs maintenance.

During a normal week, things pile up. New tasks land in your capture list. Some plans change. Projects move forward or get stuck. Notes get scribbled in odd places. By Friday the system that felt clear on Monday no longer matches reality, and a system that does not match reality is easy to stop trusting.

**A reset is not a performance review.** It is not a time to grade yourself, list your failures or wonder why you did not do more. It is a way to restore clarity. Think of it like tidying a kitchen after cooking: not a judgement on the meal, just getting ready for the next one.

A good reset does three things:

1. **Empties** the loose ends: notes, inboxes, the capture list.
2. **Updates** the system: projects, priorities and waiting items.
3. **Rebuilds** the next week so you start Monday knowing what matters.

**Make it regular and short.** Thirty to sixty minutes, same time each week. Many people prefer Friday afternoon (closing the week) or Sunday evening (opening the next one). Choose the one you will actually keep.

**Make it pleasant.** Pair it with something you enjoy: a favourite drink, music, a particular café. A reset you look forward to is a reset you keep.

**A missed reset is not a broken system.** If you skip one, do a short version the next day, or simply do the next one. Coming back matters more than never missing.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Palesa used to restart her planner every few months, each time feeling she had "fallen off". Now she spends 45 minutes every Friday at 15:00 with a rooibos tea and her laptop. She clears her capture list, updates her projects and sets next week's top outcomes.

On the Fridays she misses, she does a 15-minute version on Monday morning. She has not restarted from scratch since.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Decide the basics of your reset:

1. **Day and time.** Pick a slot you can protect most weeks.
2. **Place.** Where will you do it?
3. **Length.** Start with 30 to 45 minutes.
4. **Something pleasant** to pair with it.
5. **Short version.** What would a 15-minute reset include if you are pressed for time?

Write these at the top of the Weekly Reset template so they are there each week.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Put your reset in your calendar as a repeating appointment with yourself, with a reminder. Treat it like a meeting you would not casually cancel.

If a week goes badly, protect the reset most of all. A rough week is exactly when you most need to restore clarity.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a weekly reset?
options: To review your performance and find failures
To restore clarity and bring your system up to date
To add as many tasks as possible
questions.explain: A reset is maintenance. It restores clarity so your system matches reality again.

questions.q: You missed this week's reset. What is the best response?
options: Do a short version soon, or just do the next one
Do a double-length reset as a penalty
questions.explain: Coming back matters more than never missing. A short catch-up or simply doing the next reset keeps the system alive.

sections.markdown:
- You understand a reset as maintenance, not a performance review.
- You chose a day, time, place and length for your weekly reset.
- You have a short version ready for busy weeks.

lessons.title: Weekly Reset Questions
lessons.summary: Work through seven questions that bring your system back in line with reality.

sections.what: Seven questions that guide your reset, from what you completed to what you should remove.
sections.why: A set list of questions means you do not have to decide how to review each week. You simply answer them in order.
sections.do: Answer the seven reset questions for the week you have just had.
sections.output: Your first completed weekly reset review

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Use these seven questions in order:

1. **What did I complete?** Start here, on purpose. Many people only notice what is undone. Listing what you finished gives an accurate picture of the week.
2. **What remains?** Tasks still open. Move them back to your lists rather than carrying them in your head.
3. **What changed?** New information, new requests, shifted deadlines, a change in health, family or work. Plans should change when reality does.
4. **What is no longer important?** Some tasks lose their reason to exist. Cross them off without guilt.
5. **What am I waiting for?** Replies, deliveries, approvals. Check your Waiting projects and decide on follow-ups.
6. **What matters next?** Looking at your goals and projects, what deserves attention next week?
7. **What should I remove?** Commitments, recurring tasks, apps, subscriptions or habits that cost more than they give.

**Before the questions, empty your inputs.** Gather loose notes, check your capture list, clear your desktop and download folders, and skim your inbox for actions. Add anything new to your Master Capture List.

**Answer briefly.** Bullet points are fine. A reset should feel lighter afterwards, not heavier.

**Be kind but honest.** "I did not get to the report because two urgent client issues came up" is useful. "I am hopeless" is not information; skip it.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Lindiwe's Friday answers:

- Completed: finished the client presentation; booked the car service; three workouts.
- Remains: expense claim; email to the school about the trip.
- Changed: her manager moved the project review forward a week.
- No longer important: the newsletter redesign (team decided to keep the current one).
- Waiting for: quote from the printer, follow up Tuesday.
- Matters next: prepare for the project review.
- Remove: the weekly webinar she never watches.

Fifteen minutes, and her next week already has a clear centre.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Weekly Reset template.

1. Spend five minutes emptying your inputs: notes, capture list, inbox, downloads.
2. Answer each of the seven questions with short bullets.
3. Move every "remains" item into your Master Capture List or the right project.
4. Cross out what is no longer important.

Notice how you feel afterwards. That feeling is the point of the reset.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Use the seven questions every week at your scheduled reset time. Keep each week's answers; after a month, scan them for patterns, such as tasks that "remain" every week or things you keep wanting to remove.

Pair the reset with the Routine Tracker to see which habits held up this week and which need a smaller version.

questions.q: Why does the reset start with 'What did I complete?'
options: To give an accurate picture of the week, not just what is undone
Because it is the easiest question
questions.explain: Starting with completions corrects the habit of only noticing what is unfinished, giving a fairer picture of the week.

questions.q: What should you do before answering the reset questions?
options: Plan the next month in detail
Empty your inputs: notes, capture list, inbox and downloads
Rate your productivity out of ten
questions.explain: Gathering loose inputs first means your answers reflect everything in play, not just what you remember.

sections.markdown:
- You know the seven weekly reset questions.
- You emptied your inputs and answered the questions for this week.
- Remaining items are back in your system, not in your head.

lessons.title: Rebuild the Week
lessons.summary: Use your reset answers to set next week's outcomes, tasks, appointments and recovery time.

sections.what: The second half of your reset: turning what you learned into a clear, realistic plan for the coming week.
sections.why: Reviewing without rebuilding leaves you clear about the past but unsure about Monday. Rebuilding means you start the week knowing what matters.
sections.do: Fill in the rebuild section of the Weekly Reset for next week.
sections.output: Your Weekly Reset Dashboard

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
With the review done, rebuild the week. Create:

- **Top outcomes:** one to three results that would make the week worthwhile. Not tasks, outcomes: "Project review prepared", not "work on project".
- **Important tasks:** the specific next actions that drive those outcomes, pulled from your Project Dashboard and Weekly Priority Planner.
- **Appointments:** fixed commitments, so you can see where time is already spoken for.
- **Projects:** which Active projects get attention this week, and which simply wait.
- **Personal commitments:** family, friends, health, home. These are part of your week, not interruptions to it.
- **Recovery time:** rest, movement, time off. Plan it in before the week fills up, not after.

**Check against reality.** Look at appointments first, estimate your usable hours (Module 7) and make sure your top outcomes fit. If they do not, reduce to fewer outcomes rather than hoping.

**Place your most important work.** Give each top outcome at least one Deep work block in your energy peak window (Module 8).

**Leave space.** Do not fill every day. Unplanned days, buffers and lighter afternoons are what let the plan survive contact with the week.

When you finish, you have a Weekly Reset Dashboard: one page that shows what this week is for. On Monday morning you do not have to decide where to begin; you already have.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Ayanda's rebuilt week:

- Top outcomes: project review prepared; spare room cleared.
- Important tasks: draft review slides (Mon deep work); gather figures from finance (Tue); clear spare room with sister (Sat morning).
- Appointments: dentist Wed 08:00; team meeting Thu 10:00.
- Projects this week: project review, spare room. Website refresh waits.
- Personal: son's football match Saturday afternoon.
- Recovery: Wednesday evening off; long walk Sunday.

Two outcomes, not seven. Ayanda finishes both.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
In the Weekly Reset template, fill in the rebuild fields for next week.

1. List appointments first.
2. Choose one to three top outcomes.
3. Add the important tasks for each, with the day you intend to do them.
4. Name which projects are getting attention.
5. Add personal commitments and at least two pieces of recovery time.
6. Check: does this fit your usable hours? Trim if not.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
On Monday, open your Weekly Reset Dashboard before anything else and use it to fill in Monday's Flexible Daily Planner. Each morning, check it again to choose that day's blocks.

Use the Routine Tracker to support the routines that hold the week together, such as your reset, planning the day and a shutdown routine. Track the minimum versions so a busy week still counts.

questions.q: Which is a well-written top outcome for the week?
options: Project review slides drafted and sent to my manager
questions.explain: An outcome describes a finished result. It is clear when it is done.

questions.q: Why plan recovery time during the rebuild?
options: If it is not planned first, the week tends to fill up and leave none
questions.explain: Planning recovery before the week fills up makes it far more likely to happen, which helps the rest of the plan hold.

sections.markdown:
- You set one to three top outcomes for next week.
- Your appointments, tasks, projects, personal commitments and recovery time are in one place.
- You have a complete Weekly Reset Dashboard and a routine to support it.

modules.title: Environment & Digital Organization
modules.summary: Reduce friction in your physical and digital spaces so starting is easier and everything you need has an obvious home.

lessons.title: Physical Environment Audit
lessons.summary: Review your desk and workspace for friction, and make the things you use most easy to reach.

sections.what: A short audit of your physical workspace: your desk, work materials, visual clutter and the items you use most.
sections.why: Your surroundings either help you start or get in the way. Changing the environment is often easier than demanding more concentration from yourself.
sections.do: Audit your main workspace and choose three small changes.
sections.output: A completed Physical Environment Audit with three changes

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Focus is affected by what is around you. A cluttered desk, missing materials or a pile of unrelated papers all add small bits of friction. Each one is minor. Together they make starting harder and distraction easier.

Review four areas:

- **Desk:** what is on your main work surface right now? How much of it do you use for the work you do there?
- **Work materials:** chargers, notebooks, pens, headphones, documents. Are they where you need them, or do you hunt for them every time?
- **Visual clutter:** anything in your line of sight that pulls attention: unopened post, other projects, laundry, sticky notes from months ago.
- **Frequently used items:** the things you reach for daily. They should be the easiest things to reach.

**Aim for "ready to start", not "perfectly tidy".** You are not designing a magazine photo. You want a space where you can sit down and begin within a minute.

**Use zones.** Within arm's reach: things you use every session. In a drawer or shelf nearby: things you use weekly. Further away or out of sight: everything else.

**Reduce what is visible.** Many people find that what they can see is what they think about. Put unrelated projects in a box or drawer, labelled, so they are out of sight but not lost.

**Make the reset easy.** A tray, basket or "landing spot" for loose items lets you clear the desk in two minutes at the end of the day.

If you do not have a dedicated workspace, apply the same thinking to a portable kit: one bag or box that holds everything you need to start working anywhere.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Thandiwe works at her dining table. Her audit showed she spent the first ten minutes of every session finding her charger, clearing breakfast dishes and moving her children's school papers.

Her three changes: a box holding laptop, charger, notebook, pen and headphones, kept on a shelf by the table; a tray for school papers on the counter, not the table; and a two-minute "clear and pack" at the end of each session. Now she starts working within a minute of sitting down.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Physical Environment Audit and sit at your main workspace.

1. Rate each of the four areas from 1 (lots of friction) to 5 (works well).
2. List what is on your desk that you have not used this week.
3. Name the items you reach for every session and where they live now.
4. Choose three small changes you can make in under 15 minutes each.

Make one change right now.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Make your other two changes this week. Then add a two-minute end-of-day desk reset to your Flexible Daily Planner as part of your last block.

At your next Weekly Reset, look at your workspace again. Has clutter crept back? If so, ask what keeps landing there, and give it a home.

questions.q: What is the goal of a physical environment audit?
options: A space where you can sit down and start within a minute
questions.explain: The aim is low-friction starting, not perfection. Ready to start beats perfectly tidy.

questions.q: Where should items you use every session be?
options: In a cupboard in another room
questions.explain: Daily-use items should be the easiest things to reach, so starting does not involve hunting.

sections.markdown:
- You audited your desk, materials, visual clutter and frequently used items.
- You set up simple zones for what you use most.
- You made at least one change and planned two more.

lessons.title: Digital Environment Audit
lessons.summary: Clear the digital friction in your desktop, downloads, tabs, email, notifications, phone and files.

sections.what: A review of the digital spaces you use every day: desktop, downloads, browser tabs, email, notifications, phone and file structure.
sections.why: Digital clutter is invisible until you need something. Then it costs time, attention and focus, often many times a day.
sections.do: Rate your seven digital areas and fix the two with the most friction.
sections.output: A completed Digital Environment Audit

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your digital environment can create as much friction as a messy desk, and it travels with you everywhere. Review seven areas:

1. **Desktop:** is it a launch pad or a dumping ground? A cluttered desktop makes every file harder to find.
2. **Downloads:** this folder often becomes a second, hidden inbox. Clear it weekly.
3. **Browser tabs:** each open tab is a small reminder of something unfinished. Bookmark, capture or close.
4. **Email:** how many unread messages? Are actions buried in your inbox instead of captured in your system?
5. **Notifications:** every ping interrupts. Which ones actually need to reach you in real time?
6. **Phone:** what is on your home screen? The apps you see first are the ones you open most.
7. **File structure:** can you find any important file within 30 seconds?

**Start with notifications.** It is usually the fastest win. Turn off everything that does not need an immediate response. Keep calls and messages from key people; batch the rest into your Communication blocks.

**Tame the phone home screen.** Put tools on the first screen (calendar, capture app, maps) and move feeds and games further away or into a folder.

**Close tabs with a rule.** Anything you want to keep goes to your capture list or a bookmark folder called "To read". Then close it.

**Do not reorganise everything at once.** Fix the two highest-friction areas first. A full digital overhaul can easily become its own distraction.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Johan's audit scores: desktop 2, downloads 1, tabs 2, email 3, notifications 1, phone 2, files 3.

He started with notifications: he turned off everything except calls, messages from his family and his calendar. Then he cleared his downloads folder, deleting most of it and filing the rest. Total time: 35 minutes. The next day he noticed he checked his phone far less, because it was not asking for his attention every few minutes.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Digital Environment Audit.

1. Rate each of the seven areas from 1 (lots of friction) to 5 (works well).
2. Note the biggest problem in each low-scoring area.
3. Pick the two areas with the lowest scores.
4. Spend 15 minutes on each now. Notifications and downloads are good places to begin if you are unsure.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Add a 10-minute "digital tidy" to your Weekly Reset: clear downloads, close or capture tabs, clear the desktop and check notification settings for any new apps.

Pick one more area to improve each week until all seven score 3 or higher. Record your new scores in the audit so you can see progress.

questions.q: Which digital area is often the fastest win to improve?
questions.explain: Turning off unnecessary notifications takes minutes and immediately reduces interruptions.

questions.q: What is the sensible approach to a messy digital environment?
options: Fix the two highest-friction areas first, then improve gradually
Ignore it; it does not affect focus
questions.explain: Fixing the worst areas first gives quick relief without turning the clean-up into a new distraction.

sections.markdown:
- You rated your desktop, downloads, tabs, email, notifications, phone and files.
- You fixed your two highest-friction digital areas.
- You added a short digital tidy to your weekly reset.

lessons.title: Build Default Locations
lessons.summary: Give important information and items one obvious home so you never have to wonder where they went.

sections.what: Default locations are fixed homes for the things and information you use often: where they always live, and where you always look.
sections.why: Searching costs time and focus, and lost information creates stress. When everything has an obvious home, finding and putting away become automatic.
sections.do: Define default locations for your ten most-searched-for items and types of information.
sections.output: Your Digital & Physical Environment Audit, complete with default locations

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Important information should have an obvious home.

Think about how often you search for something: keys, a charger, a password, a document, a photo of a receipt, the notes from a call. Each search takes a little time and a lot of attention. A default location removes the search completely, because there is only one place to look.

**One home per type of thing.** Not "somewhere in my email or maybe my notes app". One place:

- Tasks and ideas → your capture system.
- Appointments → one calendar.
- Active project files → one folder per project, inside one Projects folder.
- Receipts and paperwork → one physical tray and one digital folder.
- Passwords → one secure password manager or method.
- Keys, wallet, phone → one landing spot by the door.

**Make homes obvious.** Label folders and containers plainly. "Admin – Bills" beats a clever name you will forget.

**Keep the structure shallow.** For digital files, two or three levels of folders is usually enough. Deep nesting makes things harder to find, not easier.

**Put things back at the end.** A default location only works if items return to it. Build returning into your end-of-day or end-of-session routine.

**Write the list down.** A short list of your default locations, kept with your Productivity OS, means you do not have to remember the rules either.

When everything has a home, your environment stops asking you questions.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Busi's default locations:

- Tasks and ideas: notes app, "Inbox" list.
- Appointments: phone calendar only.
- Bills and receipts: blue tray on the shelf; scans in Documents/Admin/Receipts.
- Client files: Documents/Clients/[client name].
- Keys and wallet: bowl by the front door.
- Chargers: kitchen drawer, left side.

She printed the list and taped it inside a cupboard door. After two weeks, putting things away became automatic, and she stopped losing her keys.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
In the Digital Environment Audit, find the default locations field.

1. List the ten things or kinds of information you search for most often.
2. Give each one home. Write it as "Item → Location".
3. Do the same in the Physical Environment Audit for physical items.
4. Check for doubles. If anything has two homes, choose one.

Then create any folder, tray or landing spot that does not exist yet.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For one week, every time you search for something, ask: "Does this have a default location?" If not, give it one and add it to your list.

Write three or four environment rules from this module, such as "Phone stays in the other room during deep work" or "Downloads cleared every Friday". You will add them to your Productivity OS in the final module.

questions.q: What makes a good default location?
options: Several possible places so you have options
questions.explain: One clear home per type of item means there is only ever one place to look.

questions.q: Why build putting things back into a routine?
options: Default locations only work if items return to them
It is required by the system
questions.explain: A home is only useful if things go back to it. Returning items as part of a routine keeps the system working.

sections.markdown:
- You defined default locations for your most-searched-for items and information.
- Your digital and physical audits are complete.
- You drafted environment rules to carry into your Productivity OS.

modules.title: Build Your Personal Productivity OS
modules.summary: Bring every tool together into one simple operating system you can run, maintain and restart whenever life gets messy.

lessons.title: The 369 Productivity Loop
lessons.summary: See how every part of the system connects in one repeating loop.

sections.what: The 369 Productivity Loop: Capture → Clarify → Prioritize → Break Down → Schedule → Start → Focus → Complete → Review → Reset.
sections.why: Each module gave you a tool. The loop shows how those tools work together, so you know where you are and what comes next at any moment.
sections.do: Map each stage of the loop to the tool you built for it.
sections.output: A clear picture of your system as one connected loop

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Over eleven modules you built separate tools. Now connect them. The 369 Productivity Loop is the path work takes through your system:

1. **Capture:** everything goes into one trusted place (Module 2).
2. **Clarify:** decide what each item is: task, project, appointment, idea, reference, waiting or someday (Module 2).
3. **Prioritize:** choose what matters now with Must, Should, Could and Not now (Module 3).
4. **Break down:** turn tasks and projects into concrete next actions (Modules 4 and 9).
5. **Schedule:** give important work a place with flexible blocks, matched to your energy (Modules 7 and 8).
6. **Start:** cross the starting line with the Start Now Card (Module 5).
7. **Focus:** work in defined focus sessions in a low-friction environment (Modules 6 and 11).
8. **Complete:** finish, mark it done and write the next action.
9. **Review:** check daily what got done and what moves.
10. **Reset:** each week, restore clarity and rebuild (Module 10).

Then the loop starts again.

**You can enter the loop anywhere.** Overwhelmed? Go back to Capture. Cannot start? Jump to Start. Lost track? Reset.

**When something feels stuck, find the stage.** Most problems are a missing stage: tasks that never got broken down, priorities never set, or no reset for weeks. The loop tells you which tool to pick up.

**The loop is the system.** Not the app, notebook or template. Those are just where the loop lives.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Kabelo's Tuesday morning feels chaotic. He walks the loop:

- Capture: three new requests are in his head, not his list. He writes them down.
- Clarify: one is a project, two are tasks.
- Prioritize: one task is a Must for today.
- Break down: next action is "Email Lebo the draft budget".
- Schedule: it goes in his 11:00 Communication block.
- Start: at 11:00 he opens the file and attaches it.

Ten minutes of walking the loop turned chaos back into a plan.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Use your Personal Productivity Profile from Module 1.

1. Look at the three highest-friction areas you identified back then.
2. Match each one to a stage of the loop.
3. Write down which tool you now have for that stage.
4. Mark any stage of the loop where you still feel unsure. That is where to pay attention as you assemble your system.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
For the next week, when you feel stuck or scattered, ask: "Which stage of the loop am I missing?" Then use that stage's tool.

Keep the ten stages somewhere visible, perhaps on the first page of your notebook or as a pinned note. In the next lesson you will put the whole system into the Productivity OS Builder.

questions.q: You keep forgetting things people ask you to do. Which loop stage is missing?
questions.explain: Forgetting requests usually means they are not being captured into one trusted place.

questions.q: What is the 'system' in the 369 Productivity Loop?
options: The repeating loop of stages, wherever it lives
questions.explain: The loop itself is the system. Apps, notebooks and templates are just where it lives.

sections.markdown:
- You know the ten stages of the 369 Productivity Loop.
- You matched each stage to a tool you built.
- You can use the loop to diagnose where you are stuck.

lessons.title: Assemble Your System
lessons.summary: Make ten decisions that turn your tools into one Personal Productivity OS.

sections.what: The final build: ten choices that define exactly how your system works, from how you capture to when you review.
sections.why: Tools you do not decide to use get forgotten. Writing down your choices makes your system clear, repeatable and easy to return to after a busy patch.
sections.do: Complete all ten fields in the Productivity OS Builder.
sections.output: Your Personal Productivity OS

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
Your Personal Productivity OS is a short set of decisions. Make each one specific: what you use, where it lives, and when.

1. **Capture method:** one place for everything. "Notes app inbox list on my phone, paper notepad at my desk, emptied into the notes app daily."
2. **Priority method:** how you choose what matters. "Must, Should, Could, Not now; 1 to 3 weekly outcomes."
3. **Next-action method:** how tasks become startable. "Every task written as verb + object + clear finish before it goes on a daily plan."
4. **Daily planner:** how each day gets shape. "4 to 7 flexible blocks, planned the evening before, with one buffer block."
5. **Focus method:** how you work. "Start Now Card, then focus sessions of 25 to 45 minutes, phone in another room."
6. **Energy method:** how you match work to energy. "Deep work in my 09:00 to 11:30 peak; low-energy menu after lunch."
7. **Project dashboard:** how projects are tracked. "Project Planner, maximum four Active."
8. **Weekly reset:** day and time. "Friday 15:00, 45 minutes; 15-minute version on Monday if missed."
9. **Environment rules:** the few rules that protect your focus. "Notifications off except calls; downloads cleared Friday; keys in the bowl."
10. **Review schedule:** when you check your system. "Daily: 5-minute plan and shutdown. Weekly: reset. Monthly: review Someday and this OS."

**Use what you built.** The builder shows your saved answers from earlier modules. Choose from what has actually worked, not what sounds impressive.

**Simple beats complete.** If one decision feels heavy, choose the lightest version you would really use. You can upgrade later.

**One home for the OS.** Your finished OS should fit on one page. Keep it where you will see it.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
Nomsa's OS, short version:

- Capture: phone notes "Inbox".
- Priority: three weekly outcomes.
- Next actions: verb + object + finish.
- Daily: five blocks, planned at 17:00 the day before.
- Focus: Start Now Card, 30-minute sessions, headphones on.
- Energy: writing before 11:00; admin after lunch.
- Projects: dashboard, three Active maximum.
- Reset: Sunday 18:00.
- Environment: phone face-down in a drawer during focus.
- Review: daily shutdown, weekly reset, first Sunday of the month OS check.

It fits on an index card on her fridge.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
Open the Productivity OS Builder.

1. Review your saved answers shown from earlier modules.
2. Fill in each of the ten fields with a specific decision: what, where and when.
3. For any field you are unsure about, write the simplest option you would actually use.
4. Read the whole OS back. Does it fit on one page? If not, simplify.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Run your OS for one full week exactly as written. Do not tweak it daily; note anything that does not work and change it at your Weekly Reset.

Put your OS somewhere you will see it daily: printed by your desk, pinned in your notes app or as the first page of your planner.

questions.q: What makes a good Productivity OS decision?
options: It is specific: what, where and when
It uses as many tools as possible
questions.explain: Specific decisions are easy to follow and easy to return to. Vague ones get forgotten.

questions.q: One part of your OS feels too heavy to keep up. What should you do?
options: Choose the lightest version you would really use
questions.explain: A lighter version you actually use beats a complete version you abandon. You can always upgrade later.

sections.markdown:
- You made all ten final-build decisions.
- Your Personal Productivity OS is written in one place.
- Your OS uses the tools you built across the course.

lessons.title: Keep It Running
lessons.summary: Check your system is complete, set your maintenance rules and use the 7-Day Quick Start to restart any time.

sections.what: A final check that your system is complete, plus personal rules for keeping it running and a 7-day plan to restart when life gets messy.
sections.why: Every system will slip at some point. What matters is having a clear way back that does not require starting over.
sections.do: Check the completion criteria, write your maintenance rules and save the 7-Day Quick Start.
sections.output: A complete, maintained Productivity OS and a restart plan

sections.title: Learn
sections.markdown:
**Completion check.** Your Productivity OS is built when you have:

- A capture system
- A current priority list
- Next actions
- A daily planning method
- A focus method
- A weekly reset
- A project system
- Personal rules for maintaining the system

**Maintenance rules** are short promises to yourself about how the system stays alive. Good ones are small and specific:

- "If I miss a reset, I do the 15-minute version the next day."
- "Anything in my head for more than a minute goes into capture."
- "If a day breaks, I run Stop, Reassess, Keep, Move, Continue."
- "If the system feels heavy, I remove a step instead of quitting."

Three to five rules is plenty.

**The 7-Day Quick Start.** Use this when you are new to the system, or coming back after a break:

1. **Day 1:** Brain dump and set up your capture system.
2. **Day 2:** Set your priorities.
3. **Day 3:** Break down difficult tasks.
4. **Day 4:** Set up your Start Now system.
5. **Day 5:** Prepare your focus environment.
6. **Day 6:** Flexible planning.
7. **Day 7:** Weekly reset.

Each day takes 20 to 40 minutes. By day 7, the loop is running again.

**Falling off is part of the process.** Busy seasons, illness, travel and life changes will interrupt any system. You have not failed; you have paused. The Quick Start is your way back, and your OS is still there waiting.

sections.title: See it
sections.markdown:
After a three-week family emergency, Lwazi's system had stopped completely. His capture list was out of date, his projects were stale and he felt he had "ruined it".

He opened his OS and followed his own rule: "If I fall off, I run the Quick Start." Day 1 was a 15-minute brain dump. Day 2, three priorities. By Day 7 his reset was back on Friday afternoon. Nothing was rebuilt from scratch. He simply restarted the loop.

sections.title: Try it
sections.markdown:
In the Productivity OS Builder:

1. Go through the completion checklist. Tick each item you have; note what is missing and which module covers it.
2. Write three to five maintenance rules in your own words.
3. Add your review schedule if it is not already there.

Then read the 7-Day Quick Start and decide where you will keep it: inside your OS, printed or pinned.

sections.title: Use it
sections.markdown:
Start using your system. Tomorrow, run the loop from Capture to Complete, and on your reset day run your first full Weekly Reset with your OS beside you.

Set a monthly reminder to review your OS: what is working, what is heavy, what to remove. If you ever drift for more than a week, do not rebuild. Run the 7-Day Quick Start.

questions.q: Your system has slipped for two weeks. What is the recommended response?
options: Run the 7-Day Quick Start to restart the loop
questions.explain: The Quick Start restarts your existing system step by step. You do not need to rebuild from scratch.

questions.q: Which is a good maintenance rule?
options: If I miss a reset, I do the 15-minute version the next day
Plan every minute of every day
Review everything daily for two hours
questions.explain: Good maintenance rules are small, specific and forgiving, so they still work in a messy week.

sections.markdown:
- Your OS meets every completion criterion.
- You wrote personal rules for maintaining your system.
- You have the 7-Day Quick Start ready for any restart.
- Your Productivity OS is built. Start using your system.
